0.body: This book is a companion to CMPT 424, Operating Systems , as taught by Alan G. Labouseur at Marist. It has two subjects at once. The first subject is the course itself: the textbook material (Silberschatz, Galvin, and Gagne's Operating System Concepts , with Alan's "enhancements") as it appeared in the lecture slides, chapter by chapter, from "what is an operating system?" to disk-arm scheduling. The second subject is a specific operating system, rObSen (APP_NAME = "rObSen", version 3000, naturally), the browser-based OS written in TypeScript for the semester project. It started life as Alan's Project Zero (TSOS) and grew, over a hundred commits between August and December 2025, into something that boots, takes keyboard interrupts, loads 6502a machine code into three memory partitions, schedules processes round-robin, keeps a file system in sessionStorage, and swaps processes to "disk" when memory runs out. A good deal of rObSen was written with the help of large language models. That makes it a peculiar thing to study: it works, mostly, but nobody ever had to understand it in order to produce it. This book is the act of understanding it after the fact. Every chapter takes one more layer of the system, explains the theory that layer embodies, and then reads the actual code, line by line where it matters, as you'd read a primary source.

1.body: The chapters climb the system from the bottom up, and they follow the course's order of topics while they do it: Part Course chapters Layer of rObSen I. Foundations 1, 2 The architecture as a whole; where the "hardware" ends and the OS begins II. Hardware 1, 2, 8 source/host: clock, devices, memory, memory accessor, CPU III. Kernel 1, 2, 13 source/os: bootstrap, interrupt handler, drivers, console, shell IV. Processes 3, 4 PCB, load, run, process states; threads (or their absence) V. Main memory 8 (part one) Partitions, base/limit, the memory manager VI. Scheduling 5 Theory, then rObSen's timer interrupt and dispatcher VII. Storage 10, 11, 12 The disk device driver and its track/sector/block file system VIII. Beyond contiguous memory 8 (part two) Swapping, then paging IX. Concurrency 6, 7 Races, semaphores, deadlock, and what a single-threaded browser OS gets for free X. Virtual memory 9 Demand paging and replacement, and what rObSen's "final challenge" would require Each Part's chapters raise their own questions about the code. When those questions need a TypeScript idea that goes past the basics (variables, functions, loops, compiling with tsc), the chapter gets a TS Deep Dive sub-chapter, right after the chapter that needs it. You can skip a deep dive if you already know the topic. You can also read the deep dives on their own in order; they make a short course in the TypeScript this project actually uses.

100.body:
A union type says a value can be one of several types: var _ModeDisplayUpdater: (() => void) | null = null; "Either a function that takes nothing and returns nothing, or null." The | reads as "or." Unions show up all over the kernel: public firstRunCycle: number | null; // null until the process first runs
public swapKey: string | null; // null unless the process is on disk
private dequeueNextReadyProcess(): TSOS.PCB | null
public allocate(pid: number, size: number): MemoryAllocation | null Unions aren't only about null. Chapter 9a covers unions of literal types, like "RR" | "FCFS" | "PRIORITY".

101.body: globals.ts says: var _CurrentProcess: TSOS.PCB = null; Under strict mode (specifically strictNullChecks), that's an error: null isn't a PCB. rObSen's tsconfig.json doesn't mention strict mode, and under TypeScript 5 (what rObSen was built with) that means it's off, so in this project null and undefined are silently allowed in every type. (TypeScript 6 and later flip the default to strict, which is why they report this line; Appendix C.) That's why some declarations bother with | null and others don't: the ones that do are documentation, and the compiler is not holding anyone to them. With strictNullChecks on, the compiler forces you to handle the null case before using a value, which catches a whole category of "cannot read properties of null" crashes at compile time. The newer parts of rObSen are written as if it were on; turning it on for the whole project would surface the older places that aren't.

102.body: Given a value of type PCB | null, how do you use it as a PCB? You check, and TypeScript narrows the type inside the checked branch: public krnRunProcessByPid( pid: number, ): { success: boolean; message?: string } { const pcb = _ProcessTable.get(pid); if (!pcb) { return { success: false, message: `Error: PID ${pid} was not found.` }; } if (pcb.state === "Terminated") { return { success: false, message: `Error: PID ${pid} is not resident in memory.`, }; } pcb.resetCpuState(); pcb.markReady(); this.enterKernelMode("Run PID"); this.dispatchProcess(pcb); return { success: true }; } After if (!pcb) { return …; }, the compiler knows pcb can't be null (or undefined) for the rest of the function, so pcb.state is fine. Narrowing works with: truthiness checks: if (pcb), if (!pcb) return; equality: if (pcb !== null), if (pcb.location === "Disk") typeof: if (typeof _SchedulerQuantum === "number") (used in PCB.defaultQuantum) instanceof: if (el instanceof HTMLCanvasElement) the in operator and custom type guards, which rObSen doesn't use

103.body: if (!x) treats null, undefined, 0, "", NaN, and false all the same. That's a bug waiting to happen whenever 0 is a legitimate value, and in an OS, 0 is a very legitimate value: PID 0, partition 0, address 0, priority 0. rObSen mostly avoids the trap. For example, shellRun checks Number.isNaN(pid) rather than !pid, so run 0 works. But it's the first thing to suspect when "process 0 is treated as missing."

104.body:
a?.b means "if a is null or undefined, the whole expression is undefined; otherwise it's a.b." It short-circuits instead of throwing. rObSen uses three forms: _ReadyQueue?.remove((queued: TSOS.PCB) => queued.pid === pcb.pid); // optional method call
_MemoryManager?.releaseByPid(pid); // same
_ModeDisplayUpdater?.(); // optional *function* call
readyMap.get(pcb.pid)?.toString() // optional call on a maybe-value The third one is worth staring at: ?.() calls a function only if the function exists. Without it you'd write if (_ModeDisplayUpdater) { _ModeDisplayUpdater(); }. Optional chaining is a tool for values that are legitimately sometimes absent. It can also hide bugs: _ReadyQueue?.remove(…) silently does nothing if the ready queue was never created, which would be a serious error in a running kernel. Use ?. where absence is normal, and let it crash (or check and trap) where absence means something's broken.

11.body:
The slides offer several definitions and then admit that none of them wins (slides pp. 7–19): An OS is "a program that acts as an intermediary between a user of a computer and the computer hardware." An OS is a resource allocator : it manages all resources and "decides between conflicting requests for efficient and fair resource use." An OS is a control program : it "controls execution of programs to prevent errors and improper use of the computer." "Everything a vendor ships when you order an operating system" is "a good approximation… but varies wildly." "The one program running at all times on the computer" is the kernel . Everything else is a system program or an application program. The goals are similarly plural: execute user programs and make problems easier to solve, make the computer convenient, use the hardware efficiently, manage resources, hide the complexity of the underlying hardware , and "generally implement a layered architecture." That last pair is the theme of this whole book. An operating system is an exercise in hiding things. rObSen's shell has no idea that the disk is really a JSON array in sessionStorage; the disk driver hides it. User programs have no idea which 256-byte partition they live in; the memory accessor hides it. Each layer offers the layer above it a simpler machine than the one it is standing on. Slide p. 17: users, application programs, the OS, and hardware.
Slide p. 21: the multiprogrammed memory layout, annotated "Your OS — 768." The four-component picture (users → applications → OS → hardware) maps onto rObSen like this. The hardware is the host: Cpu, Memory, MemoryAccessor, Devices. The operating system is everything in source/os/. The application programs are the 6502a hex programs you paste into the input box. The user is you at the keyboard, or GLaDOS pretending to be you.

111.body: Recall from Chapter 3 that the host's keyboard "hardware" enqueues Interrupt(KEYBOARD_IRQ, [keyCode, shiftKey, ctrlOrMeta]). The key code is a number identifying a physical key, not a character. Key 65 is the A key whether or not Shift is held. Turning (65, shift) into "A" and (65, no shift) into "a" is the driver's job.
111.breadcrumbs: Device Drivers: The Keyboard » What the hardware hands over
111.title: What the hardware hands over

112.body:
Control keys are handled first and return early. Backspace (8), Tab (9), Up (38), and Down (40) become tokens : the strings "[BS]", "[TAB]", "[UP]", "[DOWN]". Enter (13) becomes the character with code 13, a carriage return. Space (32) becomes " ". Ctrl-C (key 67 with Ctrl held, or ⌘ on a Mac, since hostOnKeypress passes ctrlKey || metaKey) becomes "[CTRL_C]". The console turns that into "kill the running process" (Chapter 8). Letters (65–90): the key codes happen to equal the ASCII codes of the uppercase letters, and lowercase letters are exactly 32 higher in ASCII. So unshifted is keyCode + 32, shifted is keyCode itself. Digits (48–57): unshifted, the key code is the ASCII digit. Shifted, the driver indexes into the string ")!@#$%^&*(", which is the US keyboard's shifted digit row starting from 0. shiftedDigits[keyCode - 48] picks the right symbol. Punctuation : a Map from key code to a [unshifted, shifted] pair. Key 186 is ;/:, 222 is '/", and so on. Anything else (function keys, Escape, Left/Right arrows, Caps Lock) is silently ignored. The result goes onto _KernelInputQueue, and the kernel's interrupt handler immediately calls _StdIn.handleInput() to consume it (Chapter 6). Note
The punctuation codes (186, 187, 188, …) are what Chrome and Safari report for a US layout. Firefox historically reported different codes for a few keys (59 for semicolon, 61 for equals, 173 for minus), so in Firefox those keys may do nothing. This is exactly the "peculiarities of hardware devices" (slide p. 73) a driver exists to absorb. Modern code would read event.key, which the browser has already translated using the user's actual layout.

113.body: Look at the input queue's contents after typing l, s, Backspace, s, Enter: "l", "s", "[BS]", "s", "\r". Characters and control tokens share one queue, distinguished only by their spelling. That's in-band signalling : the control information travels in the same channel as the data. It works here because a single keystroke can never produce the five-character string "[BS]". But it's the same design that caused the original telephone network's famous 2600 Hz vulnerability (control tones in the voice channel), and a more careful design would queue structured events, such as { kind: "char", ch: "s" } or { kind: "backspace" }.
113.breadcrumbs: Device Drivers: The Keyboard » In-band signalling
113.title: In-band signalling

114.body:
Enter is queued as String.fromCharCode(13), the carriage return (CR), not the newline (LF, code 10). That's a fossil from the teletype, a typewriter-like terminal whose Return key physically returned the print carriage to the left margin. Which brings us to the one question in Lab 001. Lab 001
"How is your console like the ancient TTY subsystem in Unix as described in https://www.linusakesson.net/programming/tty/ ?" A sketch of an answer, from rObSen's actual code. The Unix TTY subsystem sits between a terminal device and a process, and contains a line discipline that buffers typed characters, handles editing keys (erase, kill-line), echoes input back to the screen, and only delivers a completed line to the process when Return is pressed. It also turns special characters into signals: Ctrl-C becomes SIGINT for the foreground process. rObSen's pipeline has the same shape. The keyboard driver plays the UART driver (raw key codes in, characters out). Console.handleInput is the line discipline: it echoes each character, handles Backspace by editing its buffer and the screen, handles Up/Down by recalling history, and hands the whole line to the shell only on CR. Ctrl-C is intercepted by the console and turned into "terminate the running process," which is SIGINT in all but name. The main difference is that a Unix TTY delivers lines to a separate user process through read(); rObSen's "line discipline" calls the shell directly, inside the interrupt handler, because the shell lives in the kernel.

115.body: Slide p. 113 ("APIs call device drivers") and the Chapter 11 slides on virtual file systems (p. 764) make the same point from two directions: code above the driver shouldn't care what's below it. The console never sees key codes; it sees characters and tokens. The shell never sees blocks; it calls createFile and readFile. If you swapped the keyboard driver for one that read from a serial line, or the disk driver for one backed by IndexedDB, nothing above them would change. That's the claim. Chapter 15 checks how well rObSen's disk driver lives up to it.

116.body: What does the driver enqueue for Shift+/? For Shift+5? Why does the letter case use keyCode + 32 for lowercase rather than uppercase? Add Left and Right arrow support. What would the driver enqueue, and what would the console have to learn to do? Answers "?" (key 191 maps to ["/", "?"], shifted). "%" (key 53, ")!@#$%^&*("[5] is %). Because browser key codes for letters equal the ASCII codes of the uppercase letters (A = 65), and ASCII lowercase is uppercase + 32 (a = 97). Key codes 37 and 39, enqueued as "[LEFT]" and "[RIGHT]". The console would need a cursor position within its line buffer (it only tracks the end today), and insertion and backspace would have to work at that position and redraw the rest of the line.

120.body:
In most languages, a method is permanently attached to its object. In JavaScript, this is decided at call time, by how the function is called : Call form this inside the function obj.method() obj const f = obj.method; f() undefined (in strict mode, which compiled TS uses) f.call(x) / f.apply(x, args) x const g = obj.method.bind(obj); g() obj, permanently an arrow function () => … whatever this was where the arrow was written Now look at what the keyboard driver does. this.isr = this.krnKbdDispatchKeyPress copies a reference to the method's function into a field. Later, the kernel calls it like this: _krnKeyboardDriver.isr(params); That's the obj.method() form, so this is _krnKeyboardDriver. It works, but only because of how it's called. Watch what happens if someone passes the ISR around as a callback: const handler = _krnKeyboardDriver.driverEntry;
handler(); // TypeError: Cannot set properties of undefined (setting 'status') krnKbdDriverEntry does this.status = "loaded", and detached from its object, this is undefined. (krnKbdDispatchKeyPress happens never to use this, since it only touches globals, so detaching it would be harmless. That's luck, not design.)
120.breadcrumbs: Device Drivers: The Keyboard » TS Deep Dive: Inheritance, super, and the Trouble with this » What is this, really?
120.title: What is this, really?

121.body: The disk driver, written later, sidesteps the problem for its entry routine: constructor() { super(); this.driverEntry = this.entryRoutine; this.isr = this.interruptServiceRoutine; } public entryRoutine = (): void => { this.status = "loaded"; }; public interruptServiceRoutine(params: any): void { // disk operations will be invoked directly; ISR placeholder for future use this.status = `isr invoked with ${params}`; } entryRoutine is not a method; it's a field whose value is an arrow function . Arrow functions don't have their own this. They use the this of the place they were written, and a field initializer is written "inside" the object being constructed. So entryRoutine is permanently bound to its driver, no matter how it's called. Detach it, pass it to setTimeout, hand it to an event listener: this.status still refers to the right driver. The trade-off: every instance gets its own copy of an arrow-function field, whereas ordinary methods live once on the prototype and are shared. For a class with one instance (there's one disk) that's irrelevant. Notice the disk driver's isr is still an ordinary method (interruptServiceRoutine), so the same caveat applies to it as to the keyboard's. It's never called anyway (Chapter 6: there is no disk interrupt). The other standard fix is bind: this.isr = this.krnKbdDispatchKeyPress.bind(this); bind returns a new function with this locked to its argument.

Project Part One; Labs 000 and 001. The top of the input stack is two cooperating pieces, and the header comment of console.ts insists you keep them apart: "Note: This is not the Shell. The Shell is the 'command line interface' (CLI) or interpreter for this console." The console is a device abstraction: a screen you can write text to and a keyboard you can read lines from. It does echoing, line editing, scrolling, and wrapping. It knows nothing about commands. The shell is a program that reads a line, decides what command it is, and runs it. It knows nothing about pixels. Nearly all of Project Part One lives here.

126.body: The console draws on an HTML <canvas>, using a vector font from 2007 rather than the canvas's own text routines. canvastext.ts holds a table of every printable character as a list of points, and draws each glyph as connected line segments, lifting the pen at the sentinel point [-1, -1]: public static draw(ctx, font, size, x, y, str) { var total = 0; var len = str.length; var mag = size / 25.0; ctx.save(); ctx.lineCap = "round"; ctx.lineWidth = 2.0 * mag; ctx.strokeStyle = "black"; for (var i = 0; i < len; i++) { var c = CanvasTextFunctions.letter(str.charAt(i)); if (!c) { continue; } ctx.beginPath(); var penUp = true; var needStroke = 0; for (var j = 0; j < c.points.length; j++) { var a = c.points[j]; if (a[0] === -1 && a[1] === -1) { penUp = true; continue; } if (penUp) { ctx.moveTo( x + a[0]*mag, y - a[1]*mag); penUp = false; } else { ctx.lineTo( x + a[0]*mag, y - a[1]*mag); } } ctx.stroke(); x += c.width*mag; } ctx.restore(); return total; } Alan's comment on the file: "The current version on the HTML5 canvas object has text routines that are probably far better than this. But I like the brutal low-level-ness of this." It's also a good reminder that, at the bottom, a text console is just a program that draws shapes.
126.breadcrumbs: The Console and the Shell » Drawing text the hard way
126.title: Drawing text the hard way

127.body: The console keeps every line of output in an array, lines: string[], plus firstVisibleLine, the index of the line at the top of the screen. Drawing means clearing the canvas and painting lines firstVisibleLine through as many as fit. That design makes scrolling cheap: scrolling is just changing firstVisibleLine and redrawing. public putText(text: string): void { if (text === "") return; const followOutput = this.isAtBottom(); for (let i = 0; i < text.length; i++) { const ch = text.charAt(i); if (ch === "\n") { this.advanceLine(); continue; } const w = _DrawingContext.measureText( this.currentFont, this.currentFontSize, ch, ); if (this.currentXPosition + w > _Canvas.width) { this.advanceLine(); } this.lines[this.lines.length - 1] += ch; this.currentXPosition += w; } if (followOutput) { this.scrollToLatest(); } else { this.syncCaretPosition(); } this.redrawVisibleLines(); } public advanceLine(): void { const followOutput = this.isAtBottom(); this.lines.push(""); this.currentXPosition = 0; if (followOutput) { this.scrollToLatest(); } else { this.syncCaretPosition(); } this.redrawVisibleLines(); } putText measures each character and calls advanceLine when the next one would run off the right edge. That's line wrapping, which Part Two asks for. followOutput remembers whether the view was already at the bottom; if so, new output keeps it there, and if you've scrolled back to read something, new output doesn't yank you away. The scroll [lines] command moves the view down. (A commit from September 30 notes scrolling arrived "too late for the 10 points unfortunately.")

128.body: public handleInput(): void { while (_KernelInputQueue.getSize() > 0) { const chr = _KernelInputQueue.dequeue(); if (chr === String.fromCharCode(13)) { // Enter _OsShell.historyPush(this.buffer); _OsShell.handleInput(this.buffer); this.buffer = ""; } else if (chr === "[BS]") { this.handleBackSpace(); } else if (chr === "[TAB]") { this.handleTab(); } else if (chr === "[UP]") { this.historyUp(); } else if (chr === "[DOWN]") { this.historyDown(); } else if (chr === "[CTRL_C]") { this.handleCtrlBreak(); } else { // Normal printable char this.putText(chr); this.buffer += chr; } } } This is the loop that Lab 001's TTY question is about (Chapter 7). It drains the kernel input queue one item at a time: Enter (CR, code 13): push the buffer onto the shell's history, hand it to the shell, clear the buffer. [BS] : remove the last character from both the buffer and the screen. handleBackSpace deals with the awkward case where the character being erased wrapped onto a new line: it pops empty trailing lines, trims the last character, and recomputes the cursor's x position from the remaining text. [TAB] : complete the command name. [UP] / [DOWN] : recall history. [CTRL_C] : break the running program. Anything else : echo it and append it to the buffer.

129.body: public handleTab() { const typed = this.buffer.trim(); if (typed.length == 0) return; const names = _OsShell.commandList.map((c: any) => c.command); const hits = names.filter((n: string) => n.startsWith(typed)); if (hits.length === 1) { const completion = hits[0]; const rest = completion.slice(typed.length); this.buffer += rest; this.putText(rest); } else if (hits.length > 1) { this.advanceLine(); this.putText(hits.join(" ")); this.advanceLine(); this.putText("- " + this.buffer); } else { } } public historyUp() { this.recall(-1); } public historyDown() { this.recall(+1); } private recall(dir: 1 | -1) { const recalled = _OsShell.historyPeek(dir); if (recalled == null) return; this.clearLineToPrompt(); this.buffer = recalled; this.putText(this.buffer); } private clearLineToPrompt() { while (this.buffer.length > 0) { this.handleBackSpace(); } } Tab finds every command whose name starts with what you've typed. One match: type the rest. Several: list them on a new line and redraw what you'd typed. None: do nothing. History recall asks the shell for the previous or next entry, erases the current line (by calling handleBackSpace repeatedly, which is simple and slightly wasteful), and types the recalled one. The shell side keeps the list and a cursor into it: public historyPush(cmd) { this.history.push(cmd); this.historyIndex = -1; } public historyPeek(dir: -1 | 1): string | null { if (this.history.length === 0) return null; if (this.historyIndex === -1) { this.historyIndex = this.history.length; } const next = this.historyIndex + dir; if (next < 0 || next > this.history.length) return null; this.historyIndex = next; if (this.historyIndex === this.history.length) return ""; return this.history[this.historyIndex]; } historyIndex = -1 means "not browsing." The first Up press jumps to the end of the list and steps back one. Stepping past the newest entry returns the empty string, which is how you get back to a blank prompt.

13.body: A computer is a CPU and a set of device controllers sharing a bus to memory (slides pp. 23–26). Each controller has a local buffer; the CPU moves data between memory and those buffers; and when a controller finishes, it tells the CPU by raising an interrupt . When the machine powers on, a bootstrap program , usually in ROM, "initializes all aspects of the system" and "loads the operating system kernel and starts execution" (slide p. 25). Slide p. 24: CPU, memory, and device controllers on a shared bus. In rObSen, the Start button plays the role of the power switch, and Kernel.krnBootstrap is the bootstrap: it builds the kernel's queues, starts the console, loads the drivers, enables interrupts, and launches the shell. Chapter 6 walks through it.

130.body: public handleCtrlBreak(): void { _StdOut.advanceLine(); _Kernel.krnBreakCurrentProcess(); this.buffer = ""; _OsShell.putPrompt(); } public krnBreakCurrentProcess(): void { if (!_CurrentProcess) { return; } const killedProcess = _CurrentProcess; const pid = killedProcess.pid; _CPU.pause(); this.enterKernelMode("Ctrl-C"); this.terminateProcess(killedProcess); _StdOut.putText(`Process ${pid} terminated by Ctrl-C.`); _StdOut.advanceLine(); _StdOut.putText(`ACC = ${killedProcess.acc}`); _StdOut.advanceLine(); Control.hostUpdateDisplays(); Control.setPaused(false); _RunAllMode = false; this.exitToUserMode(); } The console doesn't kill anything itself; it asks the kernel. krnBreakCurrentProcess pauses the CPU, terminates the current process (freeing its memory, removing it from the queues), and reports its accumulator. It also turns off _RunAllMode, so Ctrl-C during runall stops the whole batch rather than moving on to the next process. Compare kill <pid>, which (Chapter 13) lets the others continue.

The shell's init builds a table of commands. Each entry is a ShellCommand: a function, a name, and a description. module TSOS { export class ShellCommand { constructor( public func: any, public command: string = "", public description: string = "", ) {} }
} public init() { var sc: ShellCommand; // // Load the command list. // ver sc = new ShellCommand( this.shellVer, "ver", "- Displays the current version data.", ); this.commandList[this.commandList.length] = sc; // help sc = new ShellCommand( this.shellHelp, "help", "- This is the help command. Seek help.", ); this.commandList[this.commandList.length] = sc; …and so on for 38 commands. help simply walks this table and prints each name and description, so the help text can never fall out of sync with the commands that exist. That's the advantage of treating commands as data rather than as a long if/else chain. Note the this.shellVer, without parentheses . That's a reference to the function, not a call. Chapter 8a is about functions as values.

133.body:
public parseInput(buffer: string): UserCommand { var retVal = new UserCommand(); // 1. Remove leading and trailing spaces. buffer = Utils.trim(buffer); // 2. Lower-case it. buffer = buffer.toLowerCase(); // 3. Separate on spaces so we can determine the command and command-line args, if any. var tempList = buffer.split(" "); // 4. Take the first (zeroth) element and use that as the command. var cmd = tempList.shift(); // Yes, you can do that to an array in JavaScript. See the Queue class. // 4.1 Remove any left-over spaces. cmd = Utils.trim(cmd); // 4.2 Record it in the return value. retVal.command = cmd; // 5. Now create the args array from what's left. for (var i in tempList) { var arg = Utils.trim(tempList[i]); if (arg != "") { retVal.args[retVal.args.length] = tempList[i]; } } return retVal; } parseInput trims the line, lower-cases the entire thing , splits on spaces, and treats the first word as the command and the rest as arguments. public handleInput(buffer) { _Kernel.krnTrace("Shell Command~" + buffer); // // Parse the input... // var userCommand = this.parseInput(buffer); // ... and assign the command and args to local variables. var cmd = this.resolveAlias(userCommand.command); var args = userCommand.args; // // Determine the command and execute it. // // TypeScript/JavaScript may not support associative arrays in all browsers so we have to iterate over the // command list in attempt to find a match. // TODO: Is there a better way? Probably. Someone work it out and tell me in class. var index: number = 0; var found: boolean = false; var fn = undefined; while (!found && index < this.commandList.length) { if (this.commandList[index].command === cmd) { found = true; fn = this.commandList[index].func; } else { ++index; } } if (found) { this.execute(fn, args); // Note that args is always supplied, though it might be empty. } else { // It's not found, so check for curses and apologies before declaring the command invalid. if (this.curses.indexOf("[" + Utils.rot13(cmd) + "]") >= 0) { // Check for curses. this.execute(this.shellCurse); } else if (this.apologies.indexOf("[" + cmd + "]") >= 0) { // Check for apologies. this.execute(this.shellApology); } else { // It's just a bad command. { this.execute(this.shellInvalidCommand); } } } // Note: args is an optional parameter, ergo the ? which allows TypeScript to understand that. public execute(fn, args?) { // We just got a command, so advance the line... _StdOut.advanceLine(); // ... call the command function passing in the args with some über-cool functional programming ... fn.call(this, args); // Check to see if we need to advance the line again if (_StdOut.currentXPosition > 0) { _StdOut.advanceLine(); } // ... and finally write the prompt again. this.putPrompt(); } handleInput resolves any alias, scans the command table for a match, and executes it. If there's no match, it checks two easter eggs before declaring the command invalid: curses (stored rot13-encoded in the source, so the source file itself stays polite; typing one turns on _SarcasticMode) and apologies (sorry turns it off). These come from Alan's original, which in turn come from the game Portal . execute advances a line, calls the command function with fn.call(this, args), advances again if anything was printed, and prints a new prompt. Alan's comment above the lookup loop: "TypeScript/JavaScript may not support associative arrays in all browsers so we have to iterate over the command list… TODO: Is there a better way? Probably. Someone work it out and tell me in class." The better way is a Map<string, ShellCommand> keyed by name: constant-time lookup instead of a linear scan. (With 38 commands nobody will feel the difference, but it's the right data structure, and rObSen already uses a Map for aliases.) In the code
Everything you type is lower-cased, including arguments. write notes "Hello World" stores hello world; prompt $Robsen sets the prompt to $robsen; status Compiling shows compiling. Lower-casing makes sense for the command name, so that VER and ver both work, but not for arguments. Fix: lower-case only cmd, after splitting. In the code
Utils.trim doesn't trim a single leading space. Its regular expression is /^\s+ | \s+$/g, with literal spaces around the |. That actually means "one or more whitespace characters followed by a space at the start, or a space followed by one or more whitespace characters at the end." So " ver" (two spaces) is trimmed, but " ver" (one space) isn't, and the shell reports "Invalid Command." Try it. The fix is to delete the two spaces, /^\s+|\s+$/g, or just call the built-in str.trim(). (The long comment under the regex, explaining what each part does, describes the regex the author meant to write.) In the code
Aliases only work for bare command names. alias ll ls -a reports "Alias created: ll -> ls -a", but typing ll says "Invalid Command": resolveAlias replaces the command word with "ls -a", then looks for a command literally named "ls -a". To support arguments, expand the alias textually before parsing: replace the first word of the line with the alias's target and parse the result. Also, tab completion doesn't know about aliases.

136.body: TypeScript deep dive The shell's command table stores functions in objects. The kernel removes processes from queues by handing the queue a function. The panels are built by mapping functions over arrays. In JavaScript and TypeScript, functions are values : you can store them, pass them, return them, and call them later. Alan's comment in Shell.execute calls it "über-cool functional programming," and it's the idea that makes rObSen's most flexible code work.

138.body: public execute(fn, args?) { // We just got a command, so advance the line... _StdOut.advanceLine(); // ... call the command function passing in the args with some über-cool functional programming ... fn.call(this, args); // Check to see if we need to advance the line again if (_StdOut.currentXPosition > 0) { _StdOut.advanceLine(); } // ... and finally write the prompt again. this.putPrompt(); } fn.call(this, args) calls fn with this set to the shell and args as its first argument. It's needed because fn was stored detached from the shell. As Chapter 7a showed, a detached method called as fn(args) would get this === undefined, and commands like shellAlias that use this.aliases would crash. Method Calls immediately? Arguments f.call(thisArg, a, b) yes listed one by one f.apply(thisArg, [a, b]) yes as an array f.bind(thisArg) no; returns a new, permanently bound function (can pre-fill some) Most of rObSen's shell commands avoid the question by using the global _OsShell instead of this (for example, shellHelp loops over _OsShell.commandList), which works because there's only ever one shell.

139.body:
Queue.remove takes a function that decides what to remove: public remove(predicate: (element: any) => boolean): void { this.q = this.q.filter((element) => !predicate(element)); } and the kernel uses it with an arrow function written inline: _ReadyQueue?.remove((queued: TSOS.PCB) => queued.pid === pcb.pid); The queue doesn't know what a PCB is; it just applies whatever test it's given. That's the power of callbacks: the general-purpose code (the queue) is separated from the specific decision (match this PID). The arrow function also closes over pcb from the surrounding code: it can see the kernel's local variables even though the queue is the one calling it. A function bundled with the variables it captured is a closure . Arrow syntax in brief: (x) => x * 2 // expression body: returns x * 2
(x) => { return x * 2; } // block body: needs an explicit return
() => console.log("hi") // no parameters
(a, b) => a.pid - b.pid // two parameters

140.body: rObSen leans on the standard higher-order array methods. Each takes a callback and applies it to every element. Method Returns rObSen example forEach(f) nothing readyItems.forEach((pcb, index) => readyMap.set(pcb.pid, index + 1)) map(f) a new array of results bytes.slice(a, b).map((value) => Control.hex(value)) filter(f) the elements where f is true entries.filter((entry) => !entry.hidden) find(f) the first element where f is true, or undefined this.partitions.find((part) => part.pid === pid) findIndex(f) its index, or -1 the first free partition in allocate some(f) true if f is true for any element this.partitions.some((p) => p.pid === pid) reduce(f, init) one accumulated value total free capacity; the highest-priority PCB sort(cmp) the array, sorted in place processes.sort((a, b) => a.pid - b.pid) Two of these deserve a closer look. reduce folds an array into one value. MemoryManager.availableCapacity: public availableCapacity(): number { return this.partitions.reduce((total, partition) => { return partition.allocated ? total : total + partition.capacity; }, 0); } Start with 0; for each partition, add its capacity if it's free. Chapter 13 shows the same method selecting the highest-priority process, with the accumulator being "best so far." sort takes a comparator (a, b) => number: negative if a should come first, positive if b should, zero if they tie. (a, b) => a.pid - b.pid sorts by PID ascending. Note that sort modifies the array in place; the panel code calls it on a fresh Array.from(…) copy so it doesn't reorder the process table itself.

143.body: BrowserHost: clock & devicesHost: memoryHost: CPUKernelDriversConsole & shellProcessesMemory managerSchedulerFile systemSwapper Slides: Chapter 3, "Processes," pp. 165–221. Project Part Two. With the machine and the console working, the OS can finally do the thing operating systems are for: run programs. This chapter is about the abstraction that makes that possible, the process , and the data structure that represents one, the process control block .

144.body: "A program is a passive entity stored on disk (executable image); a process is active" (slide p. 168). The program is the recipe; the process is the cooking. One program can be several processes at once: load the same hex three times and you get three processes, PIDs 0, 1, and 2, each with its own memory, registers, and progress. A process in memory has four parts (slide p. 167): the text (code), the data section (globals), the heap (dynamically allocated memory), and the stack (function parameters, return addresses, locals). Slide p. 169: a process's address space, text at the bottom, stack at the top, heap and stack growing toward each other. A 6502a process in rObSen has only two of the four: text and data, mixed together in one 256-byte partition. The sample program in Chapter 5 keeps its variables at $50–$61, right after its code, and nothing distinguishes them from instructions except that the PC never goes there. There's no stack because the 6502a subset has no push, pop, or subroutine call; there's no heap because there's no allocator. (A program that writes over its own code is perfectly legal, and occasionally done on purpose.)
144.breadcrumbs: Processes and the PCB » Program versus process
144.title: Program versus process

145.body:
Slide p. 172: the textbook's five states. "This is close to how we'll handle this in our OS projects, but with a resident queue added and without a waiting queue."
Slide p. 187: "Our Process States," the course's version, with RESIDENT between NEW and READY. The course's state machine (slide p. 187) is: NEW : op codes are in the host (the input box). No PCB yet. load creates the PCB → RESIDENT : op codes loaded into a memory segment "but dormant." run <pid> → READY : in memory, waiting for the CPU. scheduler dispatch → RUNNING ; an interrupt sends it back to READY . BRK, halt, or kill → TERMINATED : "memory available for reuse." There's no waiting state, because 6502a programs never wait for I/O: system calls complete instantly. rObSen's PCB declares the states it actually uses: export type ProcessState = "New" | "Ready" | "Running" | "Terminated"; export type ProcessLocation = "Memory" | "Disk"; There is no "Resident". A loaded process goes straight to Ready and onto the ready queue, so the ready queue doubles as the resident list. The project spec allows this ("These can be combined if you label it carefully"). "New" exists but is held only for the instant between new PCB(…) and markReady(). Chapter 9a explains the type … = "New" | "Ready" | … syntax.
145.breadcrumbs: Processes and the PCB » Process states
145.title: Process states

146.body: "Data associated with each process" (slide p. 175): process state, process ID, program counter, CPU registers, CPU-scheduling information, memory-management information (including protection), accounting information, and I/O status information. Here is rObSen's: export class PCB { public pc: number; public ir: number; public acc: number; public xReg: number; public yReg: number; public zFlag: number; public state: ProcessState; public priority: number; public quantumRemaining: number; public segment: number; public arrivalCycle: number; public firstRunCycle: number | null; public completionCycle: number | null; public waitCycles: number; public turnaroundCycles: number; public lastStateChangeCycle: number; public location: ProcessLocation; public swapKey: string | null; constructor( public readonly pid: number, public base: number, public limit: number, public readonly size: number, segment: number, priority: number = 0, ) { this.state = "New"; this.pc = 0; this.ir = 0; this.acc = 0; this.xReg = 0; this.yReg = 0; this.zFlag = 0; this.priority = priority; this.quantumRemaining = this.defaultQuantum(); this.segment = segment; this.arrivalCycle = _CpuCycleCount; this.firstRunCycle = null; this.completionCycle = null; this.waitCycles = 0; this.turnaroundCycles = 0; this.lastStateChangeCycle = _CpuCycleCount; this.location = "Memory"; this.swapKey = null; } Grouped by the slide's categories: Slide category rObSen fields Process state state Process ID pid (readonly) Program counter, CPU registers pc, ir, acc, xReg, yReg, zFlag CPU scheduling information priority, quantumRemaining Memory management (and protection) base, limit, segment, size; location and swapKey for swapping Accounting arrivalCycle, firstRunCycle, completionCycle, waitCycles, turnaroundCycles, lastStateChangeCycle I/O status none (rObSen processes do no I/O beyond printing) The state-change methods keep the accounting honest: public markReady(): void { if (this.state === "Running") { this.quantumRemaining = this.defaultQuantum(); } this.state = "Ready"; this.lastStateChangeCycle = _CpuCycleCount; } public markRunning(): void { if (this.state === "Ready") { this.waitCycles += _CpuCycleCount - this.lastStateChangeCycle; } this.state = "Running"; this.quantumRemaining = this.defaultQuantum(); if (this.firstRunCycle === null) { this.firstRunCycle = _CpuCycleCount; } this.lastStateChangeCycle = _CpuCycleCount; } public markTerminated(): void { if (this.state === "Ready") { this.waitCycles += _CpuCycleCount - this.lastStateChangeCycle; } this.state = "Terminated"; this.quantumRemaining = 0; this.completionCycle = _CpuCycleCount; this.updateTurnaround(); this.lastStateChangeCycle = _CpuCycleCount; } Every transition stamps lastStateChangeCycle with the current CPU cycle count. When a process leaves Ready (to run, or to die), the time it spent there is added to waitCycles. When it terminates, turnaroundCycles becomes completionCycle − arrivalCycle. That's exactly the slide definitions (Chapter 5, p. 284): turnaround is "the interval from process submission to process completion," and waiting time is "total amount of time a process spent waiting in the ready queue." Project Part Three requires both, measured in CPU cycles, and the panels and ps display them live. Slide p. 177: on a switch, save state into PCB0, reload state from PCB1. Chapter 13 shows rObSen's version.

In rObSen a process is born when you type load: public shellLoad(args: string[]): void { const textArea = document.getElementById( "taProgramInput", ) as HTMLTextAreaElement | null; if (!textArea) { _StdOut.putText("Error: program input area not found."); return; } if (_CPU.isExecuting) { _StdOut.putText( "Error: cannot load new code while the CPU is executing.", ); return; } if (!_MemoryManager) { _StdOut.putText("Error: memory manager is not initialized."); return; } const rawInput = textArea.value ?? ""; const trimmedInput = rawInput.trim(); if (trimmedInput.length === 0) { _StdOut.putText("Error: no input to load."); return; } const hexAndSpaceOnly = /^[0-9A-Fa-f\s]+$/; if (!hexAndSpaceOnly.test(trimmedInput)) { _StdOut.putText( "Error: invalid character(s). Only hexadecimal bytes separated by whitespace are allowed.", ); return; } const tokens = trimmedInput.split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean); const bytes: number[] = []; for (const token of tokens) { if (token.length !== 2) { _StdOut.putText( "Error: each byte must be exactly two hexadecimal characters.", ); return; } const value = parseInt(token, 16); if (Number.isNaN(value)) { _StdOut.putText(`Error: unable to parse byte '${token}'.`); return; } bytes.push(value & 0xff); } if (bytes.length === 0) { _StdOut.putText("Error: no executable bytes were provided."); return; } if (bytes.length > _Memory.size()) { const availableBytes = _Memory.size(); _StdOut.putText( `Error: program is too large. Available memory supports ${availableBytes} bytes.`, ); return; } this.collectTerminatedProcesses(); const prospectivePid = _PidCounter; let allocation = _MemoryManager.allocate(prospectivePid, bytes.length); if (!allocation) { const victim = this.findSwappableProcess(); if (victim && _Swapper?.rollOut(victim)) { allocation = _MemoryManager.allocate(prospectivePid, bytes.length); } } if (!allocation) { _StdOut.putText("Error: insufficient memory (swap failed)."); return; } _MemoryManager.load(allocation, bytes); const pid = _PidCounter++; const pcb = new PCB( pid, allocation.base, allocation.limit, allocation.size, allocation.partition, ); pcb.markReady(); pcb.placeInMemory(); _ProcessTable.set(pid, pcb); if (_ReadyQueue) { _ReadyQueue.enqueue(pcb); pcb.noteEnqueued(); } _CurrentProcess = null; const hexBase = allocation.base.toString(16).padStart(4, "0"); _StdOut.putText( `Process ${pid} loaded at 0x${hexBase} (${bytes.length} byte${bytes.length === 1 ? "" : "s"}).`, ); Control.hostUpdateDisplays(); } Step by step: Find the input and refuse if the CPU is busy. Loading while executing would race with the running process's memory accesses (and the accessor would translate the loader's addresses; see Chapter 4). Validate (Project Part One): the text must be only hex digits and whitespace, every token must be exactly two characters, and the program must fit in memory. (It checks against all 768 bytes, not one 256-byte partition. A 300-byte program passes this check and then fails to find a partition, so the error message is "insufficient memory" rather than "too large." Worse, see the callout below.) Reap dead processes : collectTerminatedProcesses frees memory still held by any terminated process. Allocate a partition from the memory manager. If none is free, swap a process out to disk to make room (Chapter 17). Copy the bytes in (MemoryManager.load also zero-fills the rest of the partition). Assign a PID. _PidCounter++ means PIDs only ever increase and are never reused, as the spec requires: "Do not reset PIDs as they are used. The PID value should always increase." Build the PCB , mark it ready, record that it's in memory, add it to the process table (_ProcessTable, a Map from PID to PCB), and enqueue it on the ready queue. Report the PID and load address. In the code
An oversized program swaps out an innocent process. Load two small programs, then try to load 300 bytes. allocate fails (no partition holds 300 bytes), so step 4 assumes memory is full and rolls PID 0 out to disk, then tries again, fails again, and reports "insufficient memory (swap failed)." PID 0 is now on disk for no reason, even though partition 2 was free the whole time. The size check in step 2 should compare against the partition size (256), so the swap is only attempted when it could help. Process creation in real systems
UNIX splits creation into two system calls (slides pp. 188–197): fork() copies the calling process, and exec() replaces the copy's memory with a new program. Windows does both in one call, CreateProcess(). Every UNIX process except the first has a parent, which can wait() for it. rObSen's load is closest to exec without the fork: the shell (which isn't a process) loads a program image into fresh memory. There are no parent/child relationships, and therefore no process tree.

148.body: public shellRun(args: string[]): void { if (!args || args.length === 0) { _StdOut.putText("Usage: run <pid>"); return; } const pid = parseInt(args[0], 10); if (Number.isNaN(pid)) { _StdOut.putText("Error: PID must be a decimal number."); return; } if (_CPU.isExecuting) { _StdOut.putText("Error: the CPU is already executing a process."); return; } _RunAllMode = false; const runResult = _Kernel.krnRunProcessByPid(pid); if (!runResult.success) { _StdOut.putText(runResult.message); return; } _StdOut.putText(`Process ${pid} is now running.`); Control.hostUpdateDisplays(); } The shell validates the PID, makes sure the CPU isn't busy, and asks the kernel: public krnRunProcessByPid( pid: number, ): { success: boolean; message?: string } { const pcb = _ProcessTable.get(pid); if (!pcb) { return { success: false, message: `Error: PID ${pid} was not found.` }; } if (pcb.state === "Terminated") { return { success: false, message: `Error: PID ${pid} is not resident in memory.`, }; } pcb.resetCpuState(); pcb.markReady(); this.enterKernelMode("Run PID"); this.dispatchProcess(pcb); return { success: true }; } The kernel resets the PCB's saved registers to zero (so a process always starts at logical address 0), marks it ready, and dispatches it: the dispatcher copies the PCB's registers into the CPU and sets isExecuting. Chapter 13 reads dispatchProcess closely. From that moment, each clock tick runs one of its instructions.

149.body: A process ends in one of three ways: it executes BRK (00); someone kills it (kill <pid>, killall, Ctrl-C); or it crashes (an invalid opcode, a missing operand). The normal path is krnCompleteCurrentProcess, called by the CPU's BRK handler: public krnCompleteCurrentProcess(accValue: number): void { if (!_CurrentProcess) { return; } const completedProcess = _CurrentProcess; const pid = completedProcess.pid; this.terminateProcess(completedProcess); _StdOut.advanceLine(); _StdOut.putText(`Process ${pid} completed.`); _StdOut.advanceLine(); _StdOut.putText(`ACC = ${(accValue & 0xff).toString(10)}`); _StdOut.advanceLine(); Control.hostUpdateDisplays(); if (_RunAllMode && _ReadyQueue && _ReadyQueue.getSize() > 0) { const nextResult = this.krnRunAll(); if (!nextResult.success) { _RunAllMode = false; _OsShell.putPrompt(); } return; } _RunAllMode = false; _OsShell.putPrompt(); } and every path that ends a process cleanly goes through terminateProcess: private terminateProcess(pcb: TSOS.PCB): void { const pid = pcb.pid; pcb.markTerminated(); if (pcb.location === "Memory") { _MemoryManager?.releaseByPid(pid); } else { _krnDiskDriver?.releaseSwapImage(pcb.swapKey); } _ReadyQueue?.remove((queued: TSOS.PCB) => queued.pid === pid); _ProcessTable.delete(pid); if (_CurrentProcess && _CurrentProcess.pid === pid) { _CurrentProcess = null; } if (!_CurrentProcess) { _SchedulerCounter = _SchedulerQuantum; this.exitToUserMode(); } } Mark it terminated (stamping the accounting fields), release its memory (or its swap image, if it's on disk), take it off the ready queue, delete it from the process table , and if it was the running process, clear _CurrentProcess.

15.body: Slides pp. 40–43 distinguish synchronous I/O (the program waits for the I/O to finish) from asynchronous I/O (control returns at once and the OS signals completion later). rObSen's keyboard is asynchronous from the user program's point of view, though user programs never read the keyboard anyway. rObSen's disk is fully synchronous: readBlock returns the data immediately, because sessionStorage.getItem is itself synchronous. Direct memory access (DMA) (slide p. 45) lets a controller move a whole block into memory and raise one interrupt per block instead of one per byte. rObSen has no DMA. Swapping copies a whole process image with one JavaScript call, which is DMA-like in spirit.
15.breadcrumbs: What Is an Operating System? » I/O: synchronous and asynchronous
15.title: I/O: synchronous and asynchronous

150.body: "A zombie process is a process that has completed execution… but still has an entry in the process table" (slide p. 194). In UNIX, a child's entry lingers after exit so that its parent can collect the exit status with wait(); once collected, the zombie is "reaped." The project spec warns that killing the running process "should not create a zombie." rObSen avoids zombies by deleting the PCB from the process table at once. The cost is that the exit status (the final accumulator) survives only as the line printed on the console; ps can never show a finished process. A UNIX-faithful design would keep terminated PCBs until something reads their status. One path does not go through terminateProcess: an invalid opcode calls markTerminated directly and then traps. That leaves a PCB in the table with its partition still allocated, which is a zombie. It's mostly academic, since the trap shuts the OS down, but it's why shellLoad begins by reaping: collectTerminatedProcesses releases anything in the Terminated state.
150.title: Zombies

151.body: "Processes migrate among the various queues" (slide p. 181): the job (resident) queue of everything in the system, the ready queue of processes in memory and ready to run, and device queues of processes waiting on I/O. Slide p. 183: processes cycle between the ready queue, the CPU, and I/O queues. rObSen has a process table (_ProcessTable) playing the role of the job queue and a ready queue (_ReadyQueue); it needs no device queues. The long-term scheduler decides which jobs to admit into memory, controlling the degree of multiprogramming; the short-term scheduler picks which ready process runs next (slides pp. 184–185). In rObSen, you are the long-term scheduler: you decide what to load. The swapper (Chapter 17) adds a medium-term scheduler, which the textbook describes as removing processes from memory to reduce the degree of multiprogramming and bringing them back later.
151.breadcrumbs: Processes and the PCB » Queues and schedulers
151.title: Queues and schedulers

152.body: The rest of Chapter 3 covers how cooperating processes communicate (slides pp. 206–220): shared memory versus message passing ; direct communication (naming the other process) versus indirect (mailboxes, ports); Mach's message-based kernel; Windows' local procedure calls; sockets; and remote procedure calls with their client and server stubs. rObSen processes can't communicate at all: each one is sealed inside its 256 bytes, and the memory accessor folds every address back into its own partition (Chapter 4). That's perfect isolation, and no cooperation. Adding a shared-memory segment would be an interesting extension. You'd map, say, logical $F0–$FF of every process to one shared physical region. And as soon as you did, two processes could both read, add, and write the same byte, which is exactly the race condition Chapter 19 opens with.
152.breadcrumbs: Processes and the PCB » Interprocess communication
152.title: Interprocess communication

153.body: Load the same program three times, then run 1. Which partition's code runs, and what are processes 0 and 2 doing meanwhile? Why does krnRunProcessByPid call pcb.resetCpuState()? What would go wrong without it? A process is loaded at cycle 100, first runs at cycle 130, waits in the ready queue for another 40 cycles in total while others run, and completes at cycle 200. What are its turnaround and waiting times? Answers Partition 1's (base $0100). Processes 0 and 2 sit in the ready queue in state Ready. run dispatches only the one process, and outside runall mode the timer ISR doesn't switch away from it, so they stay ready until you run them. A process that had been partly run (for example, interrupted by Ctrl-C during an earlier runall, if it survived) would resume mid-program with stale registers. Resetting makes run mean "start from the beginning." It's also why the saved PC must be logical (Chapter 4): zero means the start of the process's own partition. Turnaround = 200 − 100 = 100 cycles. Waiting = 30 (before first run) + 40 = 70 cycles.

In TypeScript, "Ready" isn't only a value; it's also a type , the type whose only value is the string "Ready". Combine several with | and you get a type that admits exactly those values and nothing else: let state: "New" | "Ready" | "Running" | "Terminated";
state = "Ready"; // fine
state = "Waiting"; // error: Type '"Waiting"' is not assignable to type …
state = "ready"; // error: case matters Number literals work too. The console's history recall takes a direction that can only be up or down: private recall(dir: 1 | -1) { Pass 2 and it won't compile.

157.body: Because PCB.state is a ProcessState, every comparison against it is checked. If somebody writes pcb.state === "Terminted", the compiler reports that the comparison can never be true. With a plain string, that typo would compile and silently never match, and you'd spend an afternoon wondering why dead processes are being scheduled. The scheduler mode in globals.ts uses the same idea, written inline: var _SchedulerMode: "RR" | "FCFS" | "PRIORITY" = "RR";

158.body:
A switch over a literal union can be checked for completeness. dequeueNextReadyProcess switches on _SchedulerMode, with a default: that quietly treats anything unexpected as round-robin. Here's how to make the compiler insist every mode is handled: type SchedulerMode = "RR" | "FCFS" | "PRIORITY"; function pick(mode: SchedulerMode, queue: PCB[]): PCB { switch (mode) { case "RR": case "FCFS": return queue[0]; case "PRIORITY": return queue.reduce((best, p) => (p.priority < best.priority ? p : best)); default: { const unreachable: never = mode; // error if a mode was forgotten throw new Error(`unknown mode ${unreachable}`); } }
} In the default branch TypeScript has narrowed mode to whatever's left, which is nothing: the type never. Assigning it to a never variable is fine. Add "SJF" to the union without adding a case, and mode in the default branch becomes "SJF", which can't be assigned to never, and the compiler points straight at the missing case.

16.body: Main memory is "the only large storage medium that the CPU can access directly" (slide p. 46); everything else is secondary storage, organized into a hierarchy by speed, cost, and volatility (pp. 47–50). Caching ("copying information into faster storage") happens at every level. rObSen has exactly two levels: the 768-byte Uint8Array that is main memory, and the JSON array in sessionStorage that is the disk. The hierarchy's main lesson still shows up. The disk is volatile in a way a real disk isn't: sessionStorage lasts only as long as the browser tab, so closing the tab "loses power" on the disk too. (Reset reloads the page, but sessionStorage survives a reload, so your files survive Reset but not closing the tab.)

163.body: BrowserHost: clock & devicesHost: memoryHost: CPUKernelDriversConsole & shellProcessesMemory managerSchedulerFile systemSwapper Slides: Chapter 4, "Threads," pp. 222–267. rObSen has no threads. This chapter is still worth reading, for two reasons: the concepts are on the exams, and the absence of threads, both in the OS rObSen implements and in the JavaScript it's written in, explains a great deal about how rObSen behaves.
163.breadcrumbs: Threads, and the One Thread You Have » Threads, and the One Thread You Have
163.title: Threads, and the One Thread You Have

164.body: "So far, process has a single thread of execution. But a process is really a container for threads" (slide p. 180). A thread is an execution context within a process: its own program counter, registers, and stack. All the threads of a process share its code, data, and open files. Slide p. 226: one thread (one set of registers, one stack) versus three threads sharing code, data, and files. The Windows-internals slides (pp. 200–201) put it crisply: "threads run, processes don't run." The process is the unit of resource ownership (address space, handles, security token); the thread is the unit of scheduling . Why bother with more than one? Responsiveness (the UI thread keeps responding while another thread works), resource sharing (threads share memory for free, unlike processes, which need IPC), economy (creating a thread is much cheaper than creating a process), and scalability (threads can run on different cores at once). In rObSen terms, a thread would be "the part of a PCB that the CPU loads": pc, acc, xReg, yReg, zFlag. Everything else in the PCB (base, limit, segment, location) is process-wide. A multithreaded rObSen would split the PCB into a process control block holding the memory information and a list of thread control blocks holding register sets, and the scheduler's ready queue would hold TCBs. A 6502a program would need some way to start a second thread (a new system call, say X = 03: "start a thread at address Y"), and then two threads would share their process's 256 bytes. That's precisely the situation in which the race conditions of Chapter 19 appear.
164.breadcrumbs: Threads, and the One Thread You Have » What a thread is
164.title: What a thread is

165.body: Slide p. 232: concurrent execution on one core (tasks interleaved) versus parallel execution on two cores (tasks truly simultaneous). "Parallelism implies a system can perform more than one task simultaneously. Concurrency supports more than one task making progress" (slide p. 227). A single core can be concurrent by interleaving; only multiple cores can be parallel. rObSen is concurrent and never parallel. runall interleaves three processes six instructions at a time, but at every instant exactly one instruction of one process is executing. That's the left half of the slide. Alan's comment in hostBtnStartOS_click points at the right half: "We could simulate multi-core systems by instantiating more than one instance of the CPU here." You'd need one _CurrentProcess per CPU, a scheduler that fills idle CPUs, and a clock pulse that steps every CPU. Even then, it would be simulated parallelism, because of the next section.
165.breadcrumbs: Threads, and the One Thread You Have » Concurrency versus parallelism
165.title: Concurrency versus parallelism

166.body: JavaScript in a browser page runs on a single thread , the main thread. Everything in rObSen happens on it: the clock callback, the kernel, the CPU's instruction cycle, the keyboard handler, the shell, the panels' repainting, and GLaDOS's timed keystrokes. They never run at the same time. Each callback runs to completion, and then the browser picks the next one. Chapter 10a explains the mechanism, the event loop . That has consequences you can feel: The OS can't be interrupted in the middle of anything. A keystroke that arrives while krnTimerISR is halfway through a context switch is simply queued by the browser until the ISR returns. So rObSen never needs to disable interrupts around critical sections: the language already guarantees mutual exclusion between every pair of callbacks. That's why Chapter 19 calls the kernel "one big critical section." An infinite loop in the OS freezes everything , including the clock. If a shell command looped forever, setInterval could never call hostClockPulse again, the CPU would stop, and the page would hang until the browser offered to kill it. (An infinite loop in a 6502a program is harmless, because each instruction is one short callback.) The clock is a request, not a guarantee. setInterval(…, 100) asks for a callback roughly every 100 ms. If a tick takes longer (the disk panel parsing its JSON, a long ps), the next one is late. And browsers throttle timers in background tabs, typically to about once per second, so rObSen's 10 Hz CPU slows to roughly 1 Hz when you switch tabs. Measured in cycles, nothing changes; measured in seconds, a lot does. In the vocabulary of the slides, rObSen is a many-to-one system (p. 240): many simulated activities (the CPU, the kernel, the devices, GLaDOS) mapped onto one real thread. The slide's example of many-to-one is "green threads," lightweight threads scheduled by a library rather than the OS, and that's an apt description of how the browser schedules rObSen's callbacks.
166.breadcrumbs: Threads, and the One Thread You Have » The one thread you really have
166.title: The one thread you really have

167.body: For the exams, the rest of the chapter in brief: User threads are managed by a library in user space; kernel threads are managed by the OS (p. 237–238). Many-to-one (many user threads on one kernel thread): cheap, but one blocking call blocks them all, and they can't use multiple cores. One-to-one (Windows, Linux): each user thread is a kernel thread, so true parallelism, but creation costs more. Many-to-many : the OS creates "a sufficient number" of kernel threads for many user threads. The two-level model is many-to-many plus the option to bind a user thread to a kernel thread (pp. 239–247). Thread libraries : POSIX Pthreads, Win32 threads, Java threads (pp. 248–250). Implicit threading leaves thread creation to compilers and runtimes: thread pools , OpenMP (#pragma omp parallel for), Grand Central Dispatch (pp. 251–253). Threading issues : does fork() copy all threads or only the caller?; asynchronous cancellation (kill the target now) versus deferred cancellation (the target checks periodically whether it should stop); thread-local storage (pp. 254–258). Windows threads are described by ETHREAD, KTHREAD, and TEB structures; Linux calls them tasks and creates them with clone(), which can share the parent's address space (pp. 259–266).
167.breadcrumbs: Threads, and the One Thread You Have » Multithreading models and libraries
167.title: Multithreading models and libraries

168.body:
If a fraction S of a program is serial and the rest is perfectly parallel, then on N cores the best possible speedup is speedup ≤ 1 / (S + (1 − S) / N) The slide's example (p. 235): 75% parallel, 25% serial, on 2 cores: 1 / (0.25 + 0.75/2) = 1 / 0.625 = 1.6× . As N goes to infinity, the speedup approaches 1/ S = 4×, no matter how many cores you add. "Serial portion of an application has disproportionate effect on performance gained by adding additional cores." Exam-style
A program is 90% parallelizable. What's the speedup on 4 cores? On 16? What's the ceiling? 4 cores: 1 / (0.1 + 0.9/4) = 1 / 0.325 ≈ 3.08×. 16 cores: 1 / (0.1 + 0.9/16) = 1 / 0.15625 = 6.4×. Ceiling: 1 / 0.1 = 10×. Quadrupling the cores from 4 to 16 only roughly doubles the speedup. The slide also mentions Gustafson's Law , the counterpoint: in practice, people use more cores to solve bigger problems in the same time, and the parallel part of a program tends to grow with the problem size while the serial part doesn't. Amdahl fixes the problem and asks how fast; Gustafson fixes the time and asks how big.
168.breadcrumbs: Threads, and the One Thread You Have » Amdahl's Law
168.title: Amdahl's Law

169.body: Why does rObSen never need to "disable interrupts" around its scheduler's critical sections? Switch to another tab during a long runall and come back a minute later. Has the turnaround time (in cycles) of the running processes changed compared with staying on the tab? Has the elapsed wall-clock time? Which fields of rObSen's PCB would move into a thread control block in a multithreaded design? Answers Because JavaScript runs each callback to completion on a single thread. A keyboard event can't be delivered until the current clock callback (and everything it calls) has returned. Cycles: no, because turnaround and wait are counted in CPU cycles, and cycles are counted per tick no matter how far apart the ticks are. Wall-clock: yes, much longer, because background tabs throttle setInterval. pc, ir, acc, xReg, yReg, zFlag, and the per-thread scheduling fields (state, priority, quantumRemaining, the timing fields). pid, base, limit, segment, size, location, and swapKey stay with the process.
169.breadcrumbs: Threads, and the One Thread You Have » Check yourself
169.title: Check yourself

17.body:
Multiprogramming keeps several jobs in memory so the CPU always has one to run; timesharing switches among them so often that users can interact with each (slide p. 51). That's Project Part Three: three programs in memory at once, switched round-robin. Then the most important hardware feature for protection: dual-mode operation (slides pp. 54–56). A mode bit , provided by the hardware, distinguishes kernel mode from user mode. Privileged instructions run only in kernel mode. A system call switches to kernel mode; returning from it switches back. And a timer lets the OS regain control from a process that would otherwise run forever: "set interrupt after specific period; operating system decrements counter; when counter zero generate an interrupt." rObSen has a mode bit: const MODE_KERNEL: number = 0;
const MODE_USER: number = 1; var _Mode: number = MODE_KERNEL; // 0 = Kernel Mode, 1 = User Mode. and the kernel flips it on the way in and out of every handler (enterKernelMode(reason) / exitToUserMode(); Chapter 6). It is honest to say that this mode bit is informational . Nothing in the CPU checks it, because no 6502a instruction is privileged. It exists so you can watch it change in the CPU panel and the host log, and to make the structure of the kernel visible. The timer is real, though. Cpu.cycle decrements _SchedulerCounter after every instruction and raises TIMER_IRQ when it hits zero. That is slide p. 56 in eight lines of TypeScript, and Chapter 13 reads them.
17.breadcrumbs: What Is an Operating System? » Multiprogramming, timesharing, and the mode bit
17.title: Multiprogramming, timesharing, and the mode bit

170.body: TypeScript deep dive rObSen has no main function and no loop that runs forever. It boots when the page loads, and then it waits . Every bit of work it ever does happens because the browser called one of its functions: the clock callback, a key handler, a button's onclick, one of GLaDOS's timeouts. The machinery that decides which function runs when is the JavaScript event loop . Strictly speaking it's part of the runtime, not of TypeScript, but no TypeScript program in a browser makes sense without it, and rObSen's whole notion of time rests on it.
170.breadcrumbs: Threads, and the One Thread You Have » TS Deep Dive: The Event Loop, Timers, and Callbacks » TS Deep Dive: The Event Loop, Timers, and Callbacks
170.title: TS Deep Dive: The Event Loop, Timers, and Callbacks

171.body: The browser keeps a task queue : a list of callbacks waiting to run. The event loop, built into the browser, does this forever: loop: take the oldest task from the queue run it until it returns ← nothing else of yours runs meanwhile run any queued microtasks (promise callbacks; see Chapter 19a) maybe repaint the screen The crucial rule is run to completion : once a callback starts, it runs until it returns. Another event (a keypress, a timer firing) doesn't interrupt it; it's added to the queue and waits its turn. JavaScript in a page has one call stack and one thread, so there's never more than one of your functions in progress.
171.breadcrumbs: Threads, and the One Thread You Have » TS Deep Dive: The Event Loop, Timers, and Callbacks » Run to completion
171.title: Run to completion

173.body:
const id = setInterval(callback, 100); // call repeatedly, about every 100 ms
clearInterval(id); // stop const t = setTimeout(callback, 1000); // call once, after about 1000 ms
clearTimeout(t); // cancel if it hasn't fired Both return an ID (a number, in browsers) used to cancel them. That's why globals.ts has _hardwareClockID: the Start button saves the clock's ID, and Halt passes it to clearInterval. The delay is a minimum , not a promise. A timer callback is queued when its time comes, and then waits behind whatever is already in the queue. If one clock tick takes 30 ms of work, the browser still aims for a tick every 100 ms; if a tick takes 300 ms, ticks bunch up and the effective rate drops. Browsers also deliberately slow timers down: nested timeouts are clamped to at least about 4 ms; background tabs are throttled, commonly to one timer wake-up per second, sometimes less. So rObSen's "10 Hz" CPU is 10 Hz only while it's visible and the browser isn't busy. Everything rObSen measures is in cycles (_CpuCycleCount, _OSclock), not milliseconds, so the measurements are immune to this. That's a sound design, and real operating systems make the same choice: they count timer ticks, not wall-clock time, for scheduling.

174.body:
Because everything shares one thread, a long-running callback blocks everything : public shellSpin(args: string[]) { const end = Date.now() + 5000; while (Date.now() < end) { /* busy-wait for five seconds */ } _StdOut.putText("done");
} Add that as a command and type spin. For five seconds, the clock doesn't tick, the CPU doesn't step, keystrokes aren't echoed, and the page doesn't repaint; then everything catches up at once. That's busy waiting ("Are we there yet? How about now?", slide p. 28) with the worst possible consequence: on a single thread, the thing you're waiting for can't happen while you wait. The slides' alternative is to be event-driven: instead of looping until something happens, register a callback for when it happens and return. rObSen is built that way throughout, and it's why a 6502a program stuck in a loop is harmless: each of its instructions is one short clock callback, and the browser gets control back between them.

175.body:
GLaDOS uses setTimeout to space out her tests: setTimeout(function () { document.getElementById("taProgramInput").value = codeA; _KernelInputQueue.enqueue("l"); // … TSOS.Kernel.prototype.krnInterruptHandler(KEYBOARD_IRQ, [13, false]);
}, 1000); The anonymous function () { … } is a callback that runs about a second later, by which time the OS has booted and drawn its prompt. Note also that she calls krnInterruptHandler directly , bypassing the interrupt queue and the clock, and on the Kernel prototype rather than the _Kernel instance. That works only because Kernel keeps no data in its own fields. Its methods live on the prototype, and all its state lives in globals (_krnKeyboardDriver, _StdIn, _ReadyQueue), so calling the handler with this set to Kernel.prototype (Chapter 7a's call-site rule) behaves exactly like calling it on _Kernel. Give Kernel a single instance field and GLaDOS's trick would break.

178.body: BrowserHost: clock & devicesHost: memoryHost: CPUKernelDriversConsole & shellProcessesMemory managerSchedulerFile systemSwapper Slides: Chapter 8, "Main Memory — Part One," pp. 554–598. Project Part Three; Lab 011. Chapter 4 covered the hardware half of memory management: the memory accessor that translates every address. This chapter covers the software half: the memory manager , which decides which process lives where, and the theory of contiguous allocation that it implements.
178.breadcrumbs: Binding, Base/Limit, and Partitions » Binding, Base/Limit, and Partitions
178.title: Binding, Base/Limit, and Partitions

179.body: A program refers to memory addresses. At some point those addresses have to be bound to real, physical locations. The question is when (slide p. 559): When How Slide's project tag Example Compile time The compiler emits absolute addresses. Move the program and you must recompile. iP2 MS-DOS .com files Load time The compiler emits relocatable code ("42 bytes from the beginning of this module"); the loader fixes up addresses when it knows where the program goes. iP3 classic relocating loaders Execution time Binding is delayed until each access, so "the process can be moved during its execution from one memory segment to another (due to swapping, perhaps)." Needs hardware support: base and limit registers. iP4 every modern OS Slide p. 560: source → compiler → object module → linker → load module → loader → in-memory image, with compile, load, and execution time marked. The project tags tell a story. In Part Two, with one program always loaded at $0000, compile-time binding is enough: the program's addresses are physical addresses. In Part Three, with three partitions, a program might land at $0000, $0100, or $0200, so something must relocate it. And in Part Four, with swapping, a process can be rolled out of partition 0 and rolled back into partition 2, in the middle of running , so binding must happen at execution time. rObSen uses execution-time binding throughout. Programs are written as if they start at $0000; the memory accessor adds the process's base on every access (Chapter 4). Nothing about the program's bytes ever changes when it moves. That's why swapping works at all: Chapter 17's roll-in can put a process in any free partition, update its PCB's base and limit, and carry on.
179.breadcrumbs: Binding, Base/Limit, and Partitions » Address binding
179.title: Address binding

18.body: Slides pp. 66–77 list the OS's management responsibilities: process management (create, delete, suspend, resume, synchronize, communicate, handle deadlock), memory management (track who uses what, decide what moves in and out, allocate and deallocate, "policing memory access"), storage and mass-storage management, the I/O subsystem (buffering, caching, spooling, drivers), and protection and security. The section closes with kernel data structures : lists, trees, hash maps, bitmaps (pp. 75–77). Here are the ones in rObSen's kernel: Structure In rObSen Queue (FIFO list) TSOS.Queue: the interrupt queue, the input queue, the ready queue Hash map _ProcessTable: Map<number, PCB>, the process table keyed by PID Array of records MemoryManager.partitions, the partition table Byte array Memory.bytes: Uint8Array, physical memory Set runCheck's referenced: Set<string> of in-use disk blocks Bitmap none, although the "in use" flag at the start of every disk block is a bitmap spread across the disk
