258.body:
Blocks are hex digits, so text must be converted: private stringToHex(input: string): string { return Array.from(input) .map((ch) => ch.charCodeAt(0).toString(16).toUpperCase().padStart(2, "0")) .join(""); } Array.from(input) splits the string into characters; charCodeAt(0) gives each one's numeric code; toString(16) writes it in hex; padStart(2, "0") ensures two digits; join("") glues them together. "hi" becomes "6869". Decoding goes the other way: private extractData(rawBlock: string): string { const dataHex = rawBlock.slice(this.dataHeaderLength, this.blockSize); const bytes: number[] = []; for (let i = 0; i < dataHex.length; i += 2) { const byte = parseInt(dataHex.slice(i, i + 2), 16); if (byte === 0 || Number.isNaN(byte)) { break; } bytes.push(byte); } return String.fromCharCode(...bytes); } Take two digits at a time, parseInt(…, 16), stop at the first 00 (the terminator, just like a C string or the 6502a's print-string system call), and turn the codes back into characters with String.fromCharCode(...bytes). The ... is spread in a function call: it passes the array's elements as separate arguments, String.fromCharCode(104, 105). A Unicode footnote
This encoding assumes every character code fits in two hex digits (0–255). JavaScript strings are UTF-16, so a character like € (code 8364, hex 20AC) would produce four digits and shift every following character out of alignment, and an emoji is two UTF-16 code units. rObSen's keyboard driver can't type such characters, so it never arises. The robust approach is to encode text to bytes first, with new TextEncoder().encode(text) (UTF-8), and hex-encode the bytes.

26.body: The global-script style was the norm for browser JavaScript in 2008, when this project's ancestor was written. It has real advantages for a teaching OS: no build tooling, any file can reach any part of the system (which feels like poking at real hardware registers), and the compiled output is readable. It has real costs too. Every piece of state is reachable and mutable from everywhere. For example, the shell's shellLoad sets _CurrentProcess = null directly, a kernel variable, from what is conceptually user-facing code. And there's no compiler help when one layer reaches past the one beneath it. The layered architecture of the slides is a discipline the code chooses to follow, not one the language enforces.

260.body: private currentTimestamp(): string { const now = new Date(); const pad = (value: number, length: number = 2) => value.toString().padStart(length, "0"); return `${now.getFullYear()}${pad(now.getMonth() + 1)}${pad(now.getDate())}${pad(now.getHours())}${pad(now.getMinutes())}`; } pad is a small arrow function with a default parameter, defined inside the method because nothing else needs it. getMonth() is zero-based (January is 0), hence the + 1, a perennial source of off-by-one bugs.

262.body: BrowserHost: clock & devicesHost: memoryHost: CPUKernelDriversConsole & shellProcessesMemory managerSchedulerFile systemSwapper Slides: Chapter 12, "Disk Systems," pp. 786–808. The last storage chapter goes below the file system to the device itself. rObSen's "disk" has no moving parts, so most of this chapter is theory. But the theory explains why rObSen's disk is organized into tracks and sectors at all, and it ends with a sketch of how rObSen could simulate the physics if you wanted the scheduling algorithms to matter.
262.breadcrumbs: Disk Systems and Disk Scheduling » Disk Systems and Disk Scheduling
262.title: Disk Systems and Disk Scheduling

263.body: A hard disk is a stack of platters spinning at 7,200 to 15,000 RPM, with a head for each surface on an arm that moves all the heads together (slides pp. 787–788). Each surface is divided into concentric tracks ; the set of tracks at one arm position, across all surfaces, is a cylinder ; each track is divided into sectors . Reading a sector costs: seek time : moving the arm to the right cylinder; rotational latency : waiting for the sector to spin under the head; transfer time : actually reading the bits. Seek time dominates, and it's roughly proportional to the distance the arm moves. Hence the whole subject of disk scheduling: "Minimize seek time. Seek time ≈ seek distance" (slide p. 790). The OS sees the disk as "a large 1-dimensional array of logical blocks," mapped onto sectors starting at the outermost cylinder and working inward (slide p. 789). rObSen's toIndex(track, sector, block) is that mapping in reverse: it flattens a three-dimensional address into a position in a one-dimensional array.
263.breadcrumbs: Disk Systems and Disk Scheduling » How a hard disk works
263.title: How a hard disk works

264.body:
When several I/O requests are pending, the order in which the disk serves them determines how far the arm travels. The slides use the textbook's standard example: a disk with cylinders 0–199, the head at cylinder 53, and a queue of requests for cylinders 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67 FCFS serves them in arrival order. Fair, simple, and the arm swings wildly: 640 cylinders. Slide p. 792: FCFS, total head movement 640 cylinders. SSTF (shortest seek time first) always serves the closest pending request. It's SJF for disks (slide p. 793), with SJF's virtue ( 236 cylinders) and SJF's vice: a request far from a busy region can starve . SCAN , the elevator algorithm , sweeps the arm from one end of the disk to the other, serving requests along the way, then reverses (p. 795). C-SCAN (circular SCAN) sweeps in one direction only, then jumps back to the start without serving anything on the return trip, which gives more uniform waiting times, because a request just behind the head doesn't have to wait for two full sweeps (p. 797). LOOK and C-LOOK are the same, except the arm turns around at the last request in each direction instead of travelling all the way to the edge (p. 799). Slide p. 794: SSTF.
Slide p. 796: SCAN.
Slide p. 798: C-SCAN.
Slide p. 800: C-LOOK.
264.breadcrumbs: Disk Systems and Disk Scheduling » Disk scheduling
264.title: Disk scheduling

266.body: "SSTF is common and has a natural appeal. SCAN and C-SCAN perform better for systems that place a heavy load on the disk… Either SSTF or LOOK is a reasonable choice for the default algorithm," and the scheduler "should be written as a separate module of the operating system, allowing it to be replaced" (slide p. 801). That last point is the policy/mechanism separation from Chapter 2 again, and the strategy pattern from Chapter 20a. (Modern SSDs have no arm and no rotation, so seek-distance scheduling buys nothing; their schedulers focus on fairness, merging requests, and parallelism across flash channels.)

267.body: Before a disk can hold files it needs low-level (physical) formatting , which divides it into sectors the controller can read, then partitioning into groups of cylinders, then logical formatting ("making a file system"). The boot block holds the bootstrap loader. Bad blocks are handled by sector sparing: the controller quietly remaps them to spares (slide p. 802). Defragmentation (pp. 803–805) rearranges blocks so that each file's blocks are adjacent, which matters on spinning disks because it turns many seeks into one. rObSen's chkdsk defragmenter (Chapter 15) is the same idea in miniature.
267.breadcrumbs: Disk Systems and Disk Scheduling » Disk management
267.title: Disk management

268.body: "Virtual memory uses disk space as an extension of main memory" (slide p. 807). Swap space can be carved out of the regular file system (a swap file : easy to resize, but every access goes through file-system code) or live in a separate raw partition (faster, fixed size). 4.3BSD allocated swap space when a process started; Solaris 2 allocates it only when a page is actually forced out of memory. Chapter 17 looks at where rObSen puts its swap space, and finds that it's neither.
268.breadcrumbs: Disk Systems and Disk Scheduling » Swap-space management
268.title: Swap-space management

269.body: rObSen's disk reads are instantaneous: sessionStorage.getItem takes the same time for any block. So disk scheduling can't improve anything, and there's no request queue to schedule. To make the course's algorithms meaningful, you'd simulate the physics: Give the disk driver an arm position (the current track) and a request queue . Make operations asynchronous : a request is queued, and the caller (a process, or the swapper) moves to a waiting state. On each clock tick, move the arm one track toward the next request chosen by the scheduling policy (FCFS, SSTF, LOOK, …). When it arrives, perform the read or write and raise DISK_IRQ , the IRQ number globals.ts already reserves. The disk ISR wakes the waiting process (moves it back to the ready queue). That would add the waiting state that the course's process-state diagram leaves out (Chapter 9), give the kernel a second interrupt source, and make swapping cost something, which is the honest way to motivate everything in Chapter 18.
269.breadcrumbs: Disk Systems and Disk Scheduling » What it would take to make scheduling matter in rObSen

270.body: Compute SSTF's path by hand from 53. At which step is there a tie, if any? Why does C-SCAN give more uniform waiting times than SCAN? In the example, which request waits longest under SSTF? Answers 53 → 65 (12) → 67 (2) → 37 (30) → 14 (23) → 98 (84) → 122 (24) → 124 (2) → 183 (59) = 236. No exact ties: at 67, the nearest are 37 (30 away) and 98 (31 away). With SCAN, a request that arrives just behind the head as it reverses waits a little, but a request at the far end that just missed the head waits for nearly two full sweeps; cylinders in the middle get served twice as often as those at the edges. C-SCAN serves every cylinder once per sweep, in the same direction, so the maximum wait is about the same everywhere. 183: it's served last, after the arm has gone down to 14 and back up.

271.body: BrowserHost: clock & devicesHost: memoryHost: CPUKernelDriversConsole & shellProcessesMemory managerSchedulerFile systemSwapper Slides: Chapter 8 part one, pp. 569–570; Chapter 8 part two, pp. 604–606 ("Swapping after RR context switch," "Swapping in iProject 4"); Chapter 12, p. 807 (swap space). Project Part Four; Lab 100. Three 256-byte partitions hold three processes. Project Part Four asks you to "allow the OS to execute four or more concurrent user process[es]." The answer is swapping : when memory is full, copy a process's whole image out to the disk ( roll out ), give its partition to someone else, and copy it back in ( roll in ) when it's time for it to run again. This is the top layer of rObSen, and it ties together nearly everything below it: the memory manager, the disk driver, the scheduler, the dispatcher, and the PCB.
271.breadcrumbs: Swapping: Roll-Out and Roll-In » Swapping: Roll-Out and Roll-In
271.title: Swapping: Roll-Out and Roll-In

272.body:
"A process can be swapped temporarily out of memory to a backing store, and then brought back into memory for continued execution" (slide p. 569). The backing store is a fast disk, large enough for all the memory images, with direct access to them. The cost is dominated by transfer time, "directly proportional to the amount of memory swapped," and the slide puts it bluntly: "It's S L O W (relatively speaking)" (p. 604). Slide p. 605: (1) swap out process P1, (2) swap in P2.
Slide p. 606: what it looks like in a student OS: the process list shows each process's location, Memory or Disk. Swapping is why Chapter 11 insisted on execution-time binding : a process rolled out of partition 0 may be rolled back into partition 2. Because every address the process uses is logical and translated at run time, the move is invisible to it.
272.breadcrumbs: Swapping: Roll-Out and Roll-In » The idea
272.title: The idea

273.body:
module TSOS { export class Swapper { public rollOut(pcb: TSOS.PCB): boolean { if (!pcb || pcb.location === "Disk") { return false; } if (!_krnDiskDriver) { return false; } const bytes = _Memory.snapshot().slice(pcb.base, pcb.limit + 1); const key = _krnDiskDriver.storeSwapImage(bytes); _MemoryManager.releaseByPid(pcb.pid); pcb.placeOnDisk(key); return true; } public rollIn(pcb: TSOS.PCB, allocation: TSOS.MemoryAllocation): boolean { if (!pcb || pcb.location === "Memory") { return false; } if (!_krnDiskDriver || !pcb.swapKey) { return false; } const bytes = _krnDiskDriver.loadSwapImage(pcb.swapKey); if (!bytes) { return false; } _MemoryManager.load(allocation, bytes); pcb.placeInMemory(); _krnDiskDriver.releaseSwapImage(pcb.swapKey); return true; } }
} Roll out : copy the process's partition (from base to limit) out of physical memory, hand the bytes to the disk driver, which returns a key; release the partition; record in the PCB that the process now lives on disk, under that key. Roll in : ask the driver for the bytes, load them into the partition the caller allocated, record that the process is back in memory, and tell the driver to free the swap image. The PCB carries the bookkeeping, as slide p. 606 shows: location ("Memory" or "Disk") and swapKey. The Process Table panel shows a swapped process as Disk (swap-…).
273.breadcrumbs: Swapping: Roll-Out and Roll-In » The swapper
273.title: The swapper

274.body: There are two triggers. At load time, when memory is full. shellLoad asks for a partition; if there isn't one, it picks a victim and rolls it out: private findSwappableProcess(): TSOS.PCB | null { const candidates = Array.from(_ProcessTable.values()).filter( (pcb) => pcb.location === "Memory" && pcb.state !== "Running", ); if (candidates.length === 0) { return null; } return candidates.sort((a, b) => b.arrivalCycle - a.arrivalCycle)[0]; } The victim is the most recently arrived process that's in memory and not running. (With several processes loaded in the same cycle, all with equal arrivalCycle, the stable sort leaves them in process-table order, so it's the lowest PID.) At a context switch, when the next process is on disk. The timer ISR, after choosing the next process, checks its location (if (next.location === "Disk" && !this.swapInProcess(next))): private handleSwapNeeded(excludePid?: number): boolean { if (!_Swapper) { return false; } const victim = this.selectSwapVictim(excludePid); if (!victim) { return true; } return !_Swapper.rollOut(victim); } private swapInProcess(pcb: TSOS.PCB): boolean { if (pcb.location === "Memory") { return true; } let allocation = _MemoryManager.getFreePartition(); if (!allocation) { if (this.handleSwapNeeded(pcb.pid)) { return false; } allocation = _MemoryManager.getFreePartition(); if (!allocation) { return false; } } _MemoryManager.claimPartition(allocation, pcb.pid); const swapped = _Swapper.rollIn(pcb, allocation); if (swapped) { pcb.base = allocation.base; pcb.limit = allocation.limit; pcb.segment = allocation.partition; } return swapped; } private selectSwapVictim(excludePid?: number): TSOS.PCB | null { const readyArray = _ReadyQueue ? ((_ReadyQueue.toArray() as TSOS.PCB[]) ?? []) : []; const memoryReady = readyArray.filter( (pcb) => pcb.location === "Memory" && pcb.pid !== excludePid, ); if (memoryReady.length > 0) { return memoryReady[memoryReady.length - 1]; } if (_CurrentProcess && _CurrentProcess.location === "Memory" && _CurrentProcess.pid !== excludePid) { return _CurrentProcess; } return null; } swapInProcess wants a free partition; if none is free, handleSwapNeeded asks selectSwapVictim for a process to roll out, and rolls it out. The victim is the last memory-resident process in the ready queue , excluding the one coming in. Think about what that means in the timer ISR. The ISR has just put the preempted process at the back of the ready queue. So the last memory-resident process in the queue is, every time, the process that was running a moment ago. rObSen swaps out the process that just used its quantum, to make room for the one about to use the next. That turns out to be an excellent choice. Under round-robin, the process that just ran is at the back of the queue, so it's the one that will be needed again furthest in the future . Evicting the item whose next use is furthest away is precisely Belady's optimal replacement policy (Chapter 20). For round-robin, LIFO victim selection is OPT. Whether that was designed or stumbled upon (the commit message says "select swap victim (LIFO)"), it's the right answer. krnRunAll also swaps in the first process if it's on disk, and dispatchProcess has its own roll-in path for processes resumed after a kill.

276.body: Chapter 16's slide p. 807 offers two places for swap space: a file in the normal file system, or a separate disk partition. The spec says to "take a ready process and store it to the disk via your dsDD," and Lab 100 talks about "using the disk as a backing store for your swapper." Here's where rObSen's driver actually puts the image: public storeSwapImage(bytes: number[]): string { const key = `swap-${Date.now()}-${Math.random().toString(16).slice(2)}`; sessionStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(bytes)); return key; } public loadSwapImage(key: string): number[] | null { const raw = sessionStorage.getItem(key); if (!raw) { return null; } try { return JSON.parse(raw) as number[]; } catch (err) { return null; } } public releaseSwapImage(key: string | null): void { if (!key) { return; } sessionStorage.removeItem(key); } Each image is stored under its own sessionStorage key, swap-<timestamp>-<random hex>, as a JSON array of numbers. It's not on the simulated disk at all. It never occupies a track, sector, or block, it doesn't appear in the disk viewer, and it can't run out of space (because the 192 data blocks are never consulted). After the four-process run above, the TSB disk had zero blocks in use. The commit history explains why. One commit says "roll-out/roll-in now use the same new swapkey (was truncating to one block)." The first attempt stored the image in the file system, and the file system can only hold one 32-byte block per file (Chapter 15). A 256-byte process image needs at least nine data blocks with rObSen's headers. With no block chaining, the swap image was truncated, so the image was moved out of the file system entirely. The unused allocateSwapBlock and releaseBlock methods are leftovers of the original plan. In other words, this design is downstream of the missing linked allocation in Chapter 15. Fix that, and swap images could become ordinary (hidden) files, say .swap3, which is how Windows' pagefile.sys and Linux swap files work.
276.breadcrumbs: Swapping: Roll-Out and Roll-In » Where is the swap space?
276.title: Where is the swap space?

277.body:
In the code
Swap images leak. In rollIn, look at the last three lines: pcb.placeInMemory() sets pcb.swapKey = null, and the very next line calls releaseSwapImage(pcb.swapKey), which is now releaseSwapImage(null), which does nothing. Every roll-in leaves its image behind in sessionStorage. After the four-process run above, four images were still there, and they survive Reset. Fix: const key = pcb.swapKey; before placeInMemory(), then releaseSwapImage(key). In the code
ps reports swapped processes as in memory. shellPs decides the location label from pcb.segment (Mem ${segment} if it's set, otherwise Disk). But rollOut never clears segment, so a process on disk shows as location=Mem 0. The process-table panel gets it right because it checks pcb.location. Fix: use pcb.location === "Disk" in shellPs, as the panel does. In the code
A roll-in during a context switch can land in the wrong partition. This is the most serious bug in rObSen, and it only shows up with more processes than partitions and a process finishing mid-run. Chapter 4 noted that the memory accessor translates addresses whenever _CPU.isExecuting is true and there's a current process. In the timer ISR, both are true: the CPU is still flagged as executing, and _CurrentProcess is still the process being preempted. The swapper's writes (zeroing a partition, copying an image in) go through MemoryManager, which goes through the accessor, so they're translated relative to the preempted process's base.
Usually that's harmless by coincidence. When memory is full, the victim is the preempted process (as shown above), so the free partition and "the current process's base" are the same 256 bytes. But when a partition is already free (because some process just finished), no victim is needed, and the incoming process is rolled into the free partition while the accessor redirects every byte into the current process's partition. I ran five copies of GLaDOS's ip4x test program (letters a–e) through rObSen's compiled code and logged every roll-in: one of them reads in 4 -> base 256 (current is PID 3 at base 512). PID 4's image was written over PID 3's partition, PID 4's own partition stayed full of zeros, and PID 4 then executed 00 (BRK) immediately and "completed" without ever printing its final edone.
Fix: OS code should never go through address translation. In MemoryManager, write to this.memory (physical) instead of this.accessor in load and zeroPartition. With that one change, all five programs print their done lines. (Appendix C's patch includes it.)
277.breadcrumbs: Swapping: Roll-Out and Roll-In » Bugs in the swapping path
277.title: Bugs in the swapping path

278.body: Swapping moves whole processes, 256 bytes at a time, even when a process will only touch a few of those bytes before it's swapped out again. And it inherits fixed partitions' internal fragmentation: the 22-byte counting program still occupies 256 bytes, in memory and on disk. Paging (Chapter 18) breaks processes into small fixed-size pages so memory can be allocated in pieces, and demand paging (Chapter 20) swaps individual pages rather than whole processes, loading only the pages a process actually uses. The slides draw the line explicitly: "Swappers deal with entire processes… A swapper that deals with pages is a (wait for it…) pager" (p. 656).
278.breadcrumbs: Swapping: Roll-Out and Roll-In » From swapping to paging
278.title: From swapping to paging

279.body: Why does rObSen's swapper need execution-time binding, and what would break with load-time binding? Four processes are loaded and running under round-robin. PID 3 is running when its quantum expires; PID 0, at the front of the ready queue, is on disk. Which process is rolled out to make room? How many TSB data blocks would one 256-byte swap image need if the file system had linked allocation with rObSen's 4-digit headers? Answers A rolled-in process can land in a different partition from the one it left. With load-time binding its addresses were fixed for the old base; the program would read and write the wrong partition. Execution-time binding applies the current base on every access. PID 3, the process just preempted: the timer ISR has just put it at the back of the ready queue, so it's the last memory-resident process there, and selectSwapVictim takes the last. PID 0 is rolled into PID 3's former partition. (At the very start of runall, by contrast, the CPU isn't running anyone yet, so the victim is simply the last memory-resident process in the queue, PID 3 again in a four-process run.) 256 bytes = 512 hex digits; each block carries 60 digits of data; ⌈512/60⌉ = 9 blocks.

Chapter 1 asked what an OS does. Chapter 2 asks how one is put together: what services it offers, how programs ask for them, and how the pieces are arranged. It ends with virtual machines and a slide called "Your OS Architecture," which is the cue for this chapter to look at rObSen's own structure critically.
28.breadcrumbs: OS Structures and the Machine Inside the Browser » OS Structures and the Machine Inside the Browser
28.title: OS Structures and the Machine Inside the Browser

280.body: BrowserHost: clock & devicesHost: memoryHost: CPUKernelDriversConsole & shellProcessesMemory managerSchedulerFile systemSwapper Slides: Chapter 8, "Main Memory — Part Two," pp. 599–648. rObSen stops at swapping. The course doesn't: part two of Chapter 8 replaces contiguous allocation with paging , and Chapter 9 builds virtual memory on top of it. This chapter covers paging and then designs it for rObSen concretely, because seeing exactly which lines of the memory accessor and memory manager would change is the best way to understand what paging is .
280.title: Paging

281.body: Contiguous allocation needs one unbroken hole big enough for the whole process. Slide p. 608 poses the problem: processes A (4k), B (2k), and C (3k) leave holes totalling enough room for a new 9k process G, but no single hole is 9k. "Where does it fit? It doesn't. What can we do? Break it up!" Paging breaks physical memory into fixed-size frames and logical memory (each process's address space) into pages of the same size, and lets any page go in any frame (slides pp. 610–617). A page table per process records which frame holds each page. There's no external fragmentation at all (any free frame will do), and internal fragmentation is limited to the unused part of each process's last page, "on average, ½ frame per process" (p. 624).
281.title: A new problem

282.body:
A logical address splits into a page number p and a page offset d (slide p. 618). With page size 2ⁿ, the offset is the low n bits and the page number is everything above them. The page number indexes the page table to get a frame number f ; the physical address is f × page size + d . Slide p. 619: the CPU emits (p, d); the page table maps p to f; memory sees (f, d).
Slide p. 620: four logical pages scattered across eight physical frames. Exam-style
Page size 4 bytes, memory 32 bytes (slide p. 621's "small paging example"). The page table maps page 0 → frame 5, page 1 → frame 6, page 2 → frame 1, page 3 → frame 2. Translate logical address 13. Page size 4 = 2², so the offset is the low 2 bits. 13 = 1101₂: page 11₂ = 3, offset 01₂ = 1. Page 3 → frame 2. Physical = 2 × 4 + 1 = 9.
282.title: Address translation

283.body: The OS (the memory manager, not the hardware) keeps a free-frame table : one entry per physical frame, allocated or not, and which process owns it (slides pp. 622–623). To start a process of s pages, it finds s free frames, anywhere, and fills in the process's page table. The page table is part of the process's state, so it lives in (or is pointed to by) the PCB, "along with the CPU and MA stuff."
283.title: Keeping track of frames

284.body: Smaller pages mean less internal fragmentation. But they also mean bigger page tables, more page-table overhead, and less efficient disk I/O when pages are swapped, since disks prefer big transfers (slides pp. 624–625). The trade-off settles at 4 KB on most systems, with "huge pages" (2 MB, 1 GB) available for programs that map lots of memory.
284.title: Page size

285.body:
Dedicated registers are fast but few (the PDP-11 did it). Modern page tables are large, so they live in main memory, located by a page-table base register (PTBR) and a page-table length register (slides pp. 626–628). But then "every data or instruction access requires two memory accesses: one for the page table and one for the data or instruction. (Damn!)" (p. 629). The fix is a translation look-aside buffer (TLB): a small, fast, associative cache of recent page → frame mappings, searched in parallel (pp. 630–633). On a TLB hit , translation is nearly free; on a miss , the hardware (or OS) reads the page table in memory and adds the mapping to the TLB, evicting an old one by FIFO, random, LRU, or LFU. Some TLBs tag each entry with an address-space identifier (ASID) so entries from different processes can coexist, which avoids flushing the TLB on every context switch. Slide p. 633: the TLB is checked first; on a miss, the page table in memory is consulted. Exam-style
Effective access time. A TLB lookup takes 20 ns, a memory access 100 ns, and the TLB hit ratio is 80%. On a hit: 20 + 100 = 120 ns. On a miss: 20 + 100 (page table) + 100 (data) = 220 ns. EAT = 0.8 × 120 + 0.2 × 220 = 96 + 44 = 140 ns, a 40% slowdown over raw memory. At a 98% hit ratio: 0.98 × 120 + 0.02 × 220 = 122 ns. This is why TLB hit ratios matter so much, and why locality of reference (Chapter 20) makes paging practical.
285.breadcrumbs: Paging » Where the page table lives, and the TLB
285.title: Where the page table lives, and the TLB

286.body: Each page-table entry gets a valid–invalid bit : valid means the page is part of the process's logical address space, invalid means it isn't (slides pp. 634–635). Touching an invalid page traps to the OS. This replaces base/limit checking: a process can only reach frames its own page table maps, so it can't touch anyone else's memory. Chapter 20 gives the bit a second meaning: "legal, but not in memory right now." Slide p. 635: pages 0–5 valid, pages 6 and 7 invalid.
286.title: Protection: the valid–invalid bit

287.body: A 32-bit address space with 4 KB pages has 2²⁰ pages; at 4 bytes per entry that's a 4 MB page table per process . The slides give three ways to tame that (pp. 636–644): Hierarchical paging : page the page table. With a two-level table, the 32-bit address (1 KB pages in the slides' example) splits into a 12-bit outer index, a 10-bit inner index, and a 10-bit offset; only the inner tables actually in use need to exist (pp. 637–640). Linux uses three or four levels (pp. 646–647). Hashed page tables : hash the virtual page number into a table of chains, common for address spaces over 32 bits (pp. 641–642). Inverted page tables : one entry per physical frame (not per virtual page) holding (PID, page). Memory for the table scales with physical memory, not with every process's virtual space, but finding a page means searching (pp. 643–644). Alan's aside on the slide: "FAT = Frame Allocation Table?" The analogy with the disk's file allocation table (one entry per block) is exact.
287.breadcrumbs: Paging » Structures for big page tables
287.title: Structures for big page tables

288.title: Paging, designed for rObSen

289.body: In the rObSen design, translate logical address $4A for a process whose page table is [3, 7, 12, -1, -1, -1, -1, -1]. Why does paging eliminate external fragmentation but not internal fragmentation? With 24 frames and 32-byte pages, how big must a page-table entry be to hold a frame number? How many bits does a full rObSen logical address need? Answers $4A = 74 = 010 01010₂: page 2, offset 10. Page 2 → frame 12. Physical = 12 × 32 + 10 = 394 ($018A). Any free frame can hold any page, so there's never a case of "enough total free memory but no usable piece." But a process's last page is usually only partly used, and the rest of that frame is wasted, inside an allocation. Frame numbers run 0–23, so 5 bits (plus a valid bit). Logical addresses are 0–255: 8 bits, 3 for the page and 5 for the offset.
289.title: Check yourself

29.body: The OS offers services to users and programs (slides pp. 93–97): a user interface, program execution, I/O, file-system manipulation, communication, error detection, resource allocation, accounting, and protection and security. Alan tagged several of them with project parts: the UI with iP1, program execution with iP2, resource allocation and protection with iP3. For the file system he wrote a question and its answer on the slide: "Q: How are we going to do that in TypeScript/JavaScript? A: HTML5 Storage." Chapter 15 is that answer. When error detection fails badly, you get a panic (pp. 97–99: two slides of a real macOS kernel panic log). rObSen's panic is Kernel.krnTrap, which calls Console.showBSOD: public showBSOD(reason: string): void { this.clearScreen(); this.resetXY(); const lines = [ "=== Blue Screen of Death", "", "*** Hi, I'm the Kernel trying to save you from you.***", "An OS error has occured", " ", "Reason: " + (reason || "Unknown"), "", "Press the Reset button to restart the system.", ]; for (const line of lines) { this.putText(line); this.advanceLine(); } } Project Part One asks for exactly this: "Display a BSOD message (on the CLI) when the kernel traps an OS error," plus a shell command to trigger it on purpose. That's bsod [message].

29.title: Services

290.body: BrowserHost: clock & devicesHost: memoryHost: CPUKernelDriversConsole & shellProcessesMemory managerSchedulerFile systemSwapper Slides: Chapters 6 and 7, "Synchronization and Deadlocks," pp. 491–553. This is the one major topic of the course that rObSen never had to confront, and the reason is worth understanding precisely: rObSen's kernel runs on a single JavaScript thread that is never interrupted mid-function, and its processes share no memory. Take away either of those, and every problem in this chapter appears at once. So this chapter does three things: it covers the theory, it demonstrates the problems with small simulations built from rObSen's own parts, and it shows where rObSen would need synchronization if it grew.
290.breadcrumbs: Synchronization and Deadlock » Synchronization and Deadlock
290.title: Synchronization and Deadlock

291.body:
"Concurrent access to shared data may result in data inconsistency. (This is bad.)" (slide p. 492). The slides' first example is written in 6502a (p. 493): two processes each want to double the value at $10. P1 P2
LDA $10 LDA $10
ADC $10 ADC $10
STA $10 STA $10 "We are fine if they execute in serial. But if not, there could be trouble. Lost reads, lost writes, and the whole thing is a race condition." The trouble is that each process assumes "the accumulator [is] untouched while we're adding and storing," and more importantly that $10 is untouched between its load and its store. How bad is it? src/code/sims/race.ts tries every possible interleaving of the six instructions, a context switch potentially between any two, starting with $10 = 1: $ tsc --target es2022 race.ts && node race.js
final value 2: 12 schedules, e.g. AABBAB AABBBA ABABAB ABABBA
final value 3: 6 schedules, e.g. AABABB ABAABB ABBBAA BAAABB
final value 4: 2 schedules, e.g. AAABBB BBBAAA Only the two serial schedules (all of A then all of B, or the reverse) give the right answer, 4. Twelve of twenty lose one doubling entirely (a lost write : both read 1, both store 2). And six produce 3 , a value that no serial order could produce: in AABABB, A loads 1 and adds to get 2; B loads 1; A stores 2; B adds the new $10 (2) to its stale 1 and stores 3. That's a lost read mixed with a fresh one. The slides' other examples (pp. 495–502) are the same bug in other clothes: two ticket sellers who both check "seats available" before either decrements it, and the 2016 DAO hack, in which a smart contract sent a user their balance before setting the balance to zero, letting a malicious contract call back in and withdraw again and again (a "reentrancy" attack). It cost about $50 million.
291.breadcrumbs: Synchronization and Deadlock » The problem: races
291.title: The problem: races

292.body:
The fix is a critical section : a stretch of code that only one process may execute at a time (slide p. 494). The general shape (p. 503): while TRUE { acquire lock critical section release lock remainder section
} "What do these locks look like? How are they implemented?"
292.breadcrumbs: Synchronization and Deadlock » Critical sections and locks
292.title: Critical sections and locks

293.body:
Dijkstra's semaphore (p. 504) is an integer S accessed only through two atomic operations, originally named in Dutch: wait(S) / P (proberen, "try"): while (S <= 0) ; // busy wait S--;
signal(S) / V (verhogen, "increment"): S++; A binary semaphore (0 or 1) is a mutex lock : initialize it to 1, wait before the critical section, signal after. A counting semaphore allows n holders at once. Semaphores also enforce ordering: to make S1 (in P1) happen before S2 (in P2), initialize synch to 0, have P1 run S1 then signal(synch), and have P2 wait(synch) before S2 (p. 505). The catch is the word atomic . wait must test and decrement S without anyone else getting in between, which is itself a critical-section problem (p. 507). Hardware solves it with an atomic instruction (test-and-set, compare-and-swap) or, on a single processor, by disabling interrupts for the few instructions it takes. (Lamport's bakery algorithm , linked from slide p. 506, achieves mutual exclusion with only ordinary reads and writes, which is remarkable, but slow.) The while (S <= 0); loop is busy waiting , which wastes the CPU. Real semaphores instead put the waiting process on a queue attached to the semaphore and block it; signal wakes one. Chapter 19a builds exactly that in TypeScript, with promises.
293.title: Semaphores

294.body: Every kernel function in rObSen runs inside a single JavaScript callback, and JavaScript never interrupts a callback to run another (Chapter 10a). The timer ISR can't be interrupted by a keystroke; the shell's load can't be interrupted by a context switch. In OS terms, the whole kernel runs with interrupts disabled . That makes the entire kernel one big critical section, which is the oldest synchronization strategy there is (early UNIX on uniprocessors did much the same: kernel code was non-preemptible). And rObSen's user processes can't race either, because they share nothing. Every address a process uses is folded into its own 256-byte partition (Chapter 4). The slides' doubling example can't happen in rObSen. So when would rObSen need synchronization? Shared memory between processes (Chapter 9's suggested extension). Then the race above happens for real, and user programs need a lock. The 6502a has no atomic instruction, so the natural design is for the kernel to provide semaphores as system calls, say X = 03 for wait(Y) and X = 04 for signal(Y). Because system calls run in the kernel, between instructions, on the single JavaScript thread, they are automatically atomic. A process that waits on a zero semaphore would move to a new waiting state (on the semaphore's queue) instead of the ready queue, and signal would move one waiter back. Asynchronous disk I/O (Chapter 16's sketch). Once a disk request "takes time," a process can be halfway through updating a file when another process starts reading it. That's exactly the "check, then await, then act" race that Chapter 19a demonstrates within single-threaded JavaScript. Multiple CPUs (Alan's comment in hostBtnStartOS_click). Even simulated on one JavaScript thread, two CPUs taking turns instruction by instruction would let two processes interleave on shared data, and the ready queue would need protecting if each CPU ran its own scheduler.
294.breadcrumbs: Synchronization and Deadlock » Why rObSen's kernel has no races
294.title: Why rObSen's kernel has no races

295.breadcrumbs: Synchronization and Deadlock » Deadlock and starvation
295.title: Deadlock and starvation

296.body:
Slide p. 512: "5 philosophers, 1 bowl of rice, 5 individual chopsticks. Who will survive?" Each philosopher needs both neighbouring chopsticks to eat. The obvious solution (slide p. 515), wait(chopstick[i]); wait(chopstick[(i+1) % 5]);, deadlocks if all five pick up their left chopstick at once. The slides' fixes (p. 516): pick up both chopsticks inside a critical section, or allow only four at the table. A third classic fix breaks the symmetry: number the chopsticks and have everyone pick up the lower-numbered one first. Chapter 19a runs both versions: naive philosophers: DEADLOCK: nobody can eat
ordered philosophers: all 5 philosophers ate
296.breadcrumbs: Synchronization and Deadlock » The dining philosophers
296.title: The dining philosophers

297.body: "Semaphores are cool and all, but they are low-level and 'fragile'… Lots of timing problems and Heisenbugs. We need higher-level features for our higher-level languages" (p. 516). A monitor bundles shared data with the procedures that operate on it, and guarantees that only one process is active inside the monitor at a time (pp. 517–518). Java's synchronized methods are monitors (p. 519). (In JavaScript, every object is effectively a monitor for free, because only one callback runs at a time, until an await lets someone else in.) Slide p. 518: a monitor: shared data, operations, initialization code, and an entry queue.
297.title: Monitors

298.body: The second half of Chapter 6 brings in ideas from databases (slides pp. 520–532), where "all good database systems" must deal with concurrency and failure: A transaction is a sequence of reads and writes that either commits (all of it happens) or aborts (none of it does; it's rolled back ). Write-ahead logging : before changing data, write a log record (transaction, item, old value, new value) to stable storage, bracketed by <Ti starts> and <Ti commits>. After a crash, redo every transaction with a commit record and undo every one without. Undo and redo must be idempotent (doing them twice is the same as once). Checkpoints limit how far back recovery must look. Serializability : a concurrent schedule is correct if it's equivalent to some serial order. Swapping adjacent non-conflicting operations (different data items, or both reads) doesn't change the outcome, so a schedule that can be rearranged into a serial one is conflict serializable . Locking protocols enforce it: shared locks for reading, exclusive locks for writing. Two-phase locking (2PL) requires every transaction to acquire all its locks (the growing phase) before releasing any (the shrinking phase). It guarantees conflict serializability, but "does not prevent deadlock." Notice the connection to rObSen's disk: chkdsk exists because the disk driver writes the directory entry and the data block in separate steps, and a crash between them would leave the file system inconsistent. A write-ahead log would make createFile atomic.
298.title: Atomic transactions

299.body:
Four conditions must all hold for deadlock (slide p. 536): Mutual exclusion : at least one resource is non-shareable. Hold and wait : a process holds one resource while waiting for another. No preemption : resources are released only voluntarily. Circular wait : P0 waits for P1, which waits for P2, …, which waits for P0. Resource-allocation graphs (pp. 537–541) draw processes as circles and resources as boxes (with a dot per instance), with request edges P → R and assignment edges R → P. "If graph contains no cycles → no deadlock. If graph contains a cycle → if only one instance per resource type, then deadlock; if several instances per resource type, possibility of deadlock." Slide p. 540: a resource-allocation graph with a deadlock.
Slide p. 544: collapsing resources gives the wait-for graph. There are three broad strategies (p. 547): prevent or avoid deadlock, detect and recover , or ignore the problem ("used by some operating systems, including some versions UNIX!!!"). Detection (pp. 542–546): maintain a wait-for graph (Pi → Pj if Pi waits for Pj) and periodically search it for a cycle. Recovery means aborting processes, all at once or one at a time, choosing victims by priority, progress, resources held, and so on. Prevention (pp. 548–549) breaks one of the four conditions: make resources shareable where possible; require processes to request everything up front (no hold-and-wait, at the cost of utilization and possible starvation); preempt resources from a process that must wait; or impose a total order on resource types and require requests in increasing order, which makes circular wait impossible. That last one is the ordered-chopsticks fix. Avoidance (pp. 550–552) needs advance knowledge: each process declares its maximum need, and the OS grants a request only if the resulting state is safe , meaning there's some order in which every process can still finish. With multiple instances per resource, that's the banker's algorithm : "the OS does not get over-leveraged." Exam-style: the banker's algorithm
Five processes, resources A, B, C with 10, 5, 7 instances. Available = (3, 3, 2). Allocation Max Need = Max − Allocation
P0 0 1 0 7 5 3 7 4 3
P1 2 0 0 3 2 2 1 2 2
P2 3 0 2 9 0 2 6 0 0
P3 2 1 1 2 2 2 0 1 1
P4 0 0 2 4 3 3 4 3 1
Safety check: find a process whose Need ≤ Work (initially Available), pretend it finishes and returns its Allocation, repeat. P1 (122 ≤ 332) → Work 532. P3 (011) → 743. P4 (431) → 745. P0 (743) → 755. P2 (600) → 10 5 7. All finish: safe, sequence ⟨P1, P3, P4, P0, P2⟩.
Can P1's request (1, 0, 2) be granted? Pretend: Available becomes (2, 3, 0), P1's Allocation (3, 0, 2), its Need (0, 2, 0). The safety check still succeeds, so yes.
Then P0 requests (0, 2, 0). Available would be (2, 1, 0); nobody's Need fits; unsafe: P0 must wait, even though the resources are physically available.
src/code/sims/bankers.ts checks all three answers.
299.title: Deadlock, systematically (Chapter 7)

30.body: Slide p. 100 says the CLI is "sometimes, but not often, implemented in the kernel (like ours)," and then asks the right question: in Unix the shell is just a program, so adding a command doesn't require changing the shell; "We have to modify the kernel. Is this better? Should we change?" rObSen's shell lives inside the OS. Every one of its 38 commands is a method of the Shell class, registered in a table at boot, and adding one means editing shell.ts and recompiling the whole OS. That's the cost. The benefit is simplicity: rObSen has no way to load a program that acts as a shell, because user programs are 6502a machine code that can only print numbers and strings. Chapter 8 reads the shell in detail.

30.title: The command interpreter

300.body: In the race simulation, why can't the result ever be 1 or 8? Which of the four deadlock conditions does "allow only four philosophers at the table" break? Why doesn't rObSen's kernel need a lock around the ready queue, and what single change to the host would make it need one? Answers Every process stores something computed from a load of $10 (which is at least 1) plus a later load (at least 1), so the stored value is at least 2. And 8 would require three doublings, but there are only two processes, each doubling at most once. Circular wait: with only four seated, at least one philosopher can always get both chopsticks, so the cycle can't close. Because every kernel function runs to completion on JavaScript's single thread, so nothing else touches the queue meanwhile. Adding a second CPU that runs its own scheduler in an interleaved fashion (or moving the CPU into a Web Worker, a separate thread) would.
300.title: Check yourself

301.body: TypeScript deep dive rObSen doesn't use promises at all. Every operation in it is synchronous, even the disk. But the moment you want a process to wait for something (a semaphore, a slow disk, a network), you need a way to say "continue this later, when X happens" without blocking the single JavaScript thread. That's what promises and async/await are for. And they bring a surprise that ties directly to Chapter 19: single-threaded code can still have race conditions.
301.breadcrumbs: Synchronization and Deadlock » TS Deep Dive: Promises and async/await » TS Deep Dive: Promises and async/await
301.title: TS Deep Dive: Promises and async/await

302.body:
A promise is an object representing a value that isn't available yet. It's in one of three states: pending , fulfilled (with a value), or rejected (with an error). Once settled, it never changes. const p: Promise<number> = new Promise((resolve, reject) => { setTimeout(() => resolve(42), 1000); // fulfil with 42 after a second
}); p.then((value) => console.log(value)); // runs later, with 42 The function passed to new Promise (the "executor") runs immediately and receives two functions: call resolve(value) to fulfil, or reject(error) to reject. .then(f) registers a callback for when the promise is fulfilled. Promise<number> is a generic type (Chapter 13a): a promise of a number.
302.breadcrumbs: Synchronization and Deadlock » TS Deep Dive: Promises and async/await » Promises
302.title: Promises

303.body:
Chains of .then get hard to read. An async function lets you write the same thing as straight-line code: async function loadAndRun(): Promise<void> { const bytes = await readProgramFromDisk("counter"); // pause here until it's ready const pid = await loadIntoMemory(bytes); console.log(`loaded as PID ${pid}`);
} await p pauses this function until p settles, then continues with its value (or throws its error). Crucially, it doesn't block the thread: while loadAndRun is paused, the event loop runs other callbacks (clock ticks, keystrokes). An async function always returns a promise, so callers can await it in turn. Under the hood, the part of the function after an await becomes a callback, queued as a microtask when the awaited promise settles. Microtasks run after the current task finishes and before the next task (Chapter 10a's event-loop sketch).
303.breadcrumbs: Synchronization and Deadlock » TS Deep Dive: Promises and async/await » async and await
303.title: async and await

304.body:
Chapter 19's semaphore used a busy-wait loop, while (S <= 0);, which on a single thread would spin forever: nothing else could ever run to signal it. With promises, waiting means "give me a promise that will be resolved when it's my turn": class Semaphore { private waiting: (() => void)[] = []; // resolvers of blocked wait() calls, FIFO constructor(private value: number) {} /** P(): take a unit, or block (asynchronously) until one is available. */ wait(): Promise<void> { if (this.value > 0) { this.value--; return Promise.resolve(); } return new Promise<void>((resolve) => this.waiting.push(resolve)); } /** V(): give a unit back, waking the longest waiter if there is one. */ signal(): void { const next = this.waiting.shift(); if (next) next(); // hand the unit straight to the waiter else this.value++; }
} wait() with a unit available: take it, return an already-resolved promise. wait() with none: create a pending promise and keep its resolve function in the waiting queue. The caller awaits that promise and is suspended, consuming no CPU. signal(): if someone is waiting, call their resolve (handing the unit straight to them, FIFO, so no one starves); otherwise increment the count. This is the structure the slides describe for a real kernel semaphore: a value plus a queue of blocked processes, with signal waking one. The waiting array is the semaphore's device queue.

307.body: A Promise<T> is a future value: pending, then fulfilled or rejected. async functions return promises; await suspends the function (not the thread) until a promise settles. A semaphore is a counter plus a queue of resolve functions; signal resolves the oldest. Single-threaded async code can race wherever there's an await between a check and an act. Hold a lock across it. Promise.all waits for all; Promise.race for the first. A timeout race is a simple deadlock detector.

308.body: BrowserHost: clock & devicesHost: memoryHost: CPUKernelDriversConsole & shellProcessesMemory managerSchedulerFile systemSwapper Slides: Chapter 9, "Virtual Memory," pp. 649–716. Project Part Four's final challenge: "Add demand paging in place of swapping." The last chapter of the course, and the last chapter here, puts every layer of the system to work at once: the CPU must stop mid-instruction, the memory accessor must notice a missing page, the kernel must handle a new kind of trap, the memory manager must pick a victim, the disk must store pages, and the scheduler must cope with a process that's waiting for one. It's the project's "final challenge," which rObSen didn't attempt. So this chapter teaches the theory, checks the replacement algorithms with code, and then lays out the design for rObSen in enough detail to build.

308.title: Demand Paging and Page Replacement

309.body: "Up till now we have been allocating memory for the entire process. Do we have to?" (slide p. 651). Virtual memory separates the logical address space from physical memory, so that "only part of the program needs to be in memory at any one time for execution," and the logical address space can be much larger than physical memory (p. 652). Side benefits: address spaces can be shared (one copy of a shared library mapped into many processes, p. 655), and process creation gets cheaper (copy-on-write, below).
309.breadcrumbs: Demand Paging and Page Replacement » Virtual memory
309.title: Virtual memory

31.body:
A system call is the programming interface to the OS's services (slides pp. 109–124). Programs rarely invoke system calls directly; they go through an API (Win32, POSIX, the Java API) whose library routines make the actual calls. The kernel identifies each system call by a number and dispatches through a table. The caller "need know nothing about how the system call is implemented." Parameters can reach the kernel three ways (slide p. 118): In registers : simplest, but limited by the number of registers. In a block or table in memory , with the block's address in a register: Linux and Solaris do this. On the stack . Slide p. 115: user application → system-call interface → kernel implementation of open().
Slide p. 119: "This is how you're going to implement System Calls in our client OS" (iP2, iP3, iP4). The 6502a has exactly one system-call instruction, FF (SYS). The X register picks the call, and the Y register carries the argument: X = 01: print the integer in Y. (Parameter in a register.) X = 02: print the 00-terminated string starting at the address in Y. (Parameter in a block in memory, address in a register: method 2, exactly the slide.) Here is rObSen's implementation: private opSystemCall(): void { if (this.Xreg === 0x01) { _StdOut.putText(this.Yreg.toString()); } else if (this.Xreg === 0x02) { let address = this.Yreg & 0xff; let output = ""; let value = this.readMemory(address); while (value !== 0x00) { output += String.fromCharCode(value); address = (address + 1) & 0xff; value = this.readMemory(address); } _StdOut.putText(output); } else { _StdOut.putText(`[syscall x=${this.Xreg}]`); } } It works: Chapter 5 traces a program that prints A7 through these two calls. But notice where it lives. This is cpu.ts, in the host , and it reaches straight into the client OS's console (_StdOut.putText). Real hardware doesn't know what a console is. On a real machine, SYS would raise a software interrupt (a trap), the CPU would switch to kernel mode, and the kernel's system-call handler would decide what X means and do the printing. In the code
The 6502a instruction-set handout says it directly: "In the OS simulations, the CPU object will generate a software interrupt when it sees the SYS op code (FF)." rObSen's CPU instead performs the system call itself, so system calls never enter the kernel, never flip the mode bit, and can't be scheduled, logged, or protected by the OS. The kernel even has a comment block listing system calls it might someday offer (ReadConsole, WriteConsole, CreateProcess, …) with no implementation. Appendix C shows the fix: enqueue a SYSCALL_IRQ with X and Y as parameters, and handle it in krnInterruptHandler. // // System Calls... that generate software interrupts via tha Application Programming Interface library routines. // // Some ideas: // - ReadConsole // - WriteConsole // - CreateProcess // - ExitProcess // - WaitForProcessToExit // - CreateFile // - OpenFile // - ReadFile // - WriteFile // - CloseFile

31.title: System calls

310.body: "Q: When is it good to be lazy? A: When swapping memory" (slide p. 656). A lazy swapper "never swaps a page into memory unless page will be needed." Since it deals in pages rather than whole processes, it gets a new name: "A swapper that deals with pages is a (wait for it…) pager ." The mechanism reuses Chapter 18's valid–invalid bit with a broader meaning: valid means "legal and in memory"; invalid means "illegal, or legal but currently on disk" (p. 658). The OS keeps a second table (per process, in the PCB) to tell those apart. Slide p. 662: reference → trap → page is on backing store → bring in missing page → reset page table → restart instruction. Touching an invalid page causes a page fault , a trap to the OS (slide p. 661): Check the process's table: an illegal reference aborts the process; a legal one continues. Get an empty frame. Read the page from disk into the frame. Update the tables. Set the valid bit. Restart the instruction that caused the fault. The division of labour (slide p. 663, with Alan's correction that the textbook "misnames" the hardware part): the hardware (the memory accessor) maps pages to frames and checks valid bits; the OS (the memory manager) does the swapping, allocation, page replacement, and table updates. Pure demand paging starts a process with no pages in memory; its very first instruction fetch faults (p. 664). One instruction can fault more than once (the instruction on one page, its operand on another, its data on a third), but locality of reference ("scope stickiness," in Alan's phrase) makes that rare: programs tend to work on a small set of pages for a while, then move on.
310.breadcrumbs: Demand Paging and Page Replacement » Demand paging
310.title: Demand paging

311.body: When a process forks, the child's pages start out identical to the parent's. Copy-on-write (pp. 665–669) lets them share the physical pages until one of them writes, and only then copies the page being written. New pages are handed out from a pool of zeroed-out pages, "zero-fill on demand," so no process can read another's leftover data. (vm_stat on a Mac shows both counters; on the slide's machine, 75 million copy-on-write faults and 1.7 billion zero-filled pages.) rObSen's memory manager already zero-fills partitions on load and release (Chapter 11), which is the same principle at a coarser grain.
311.breadcrumbs: Demand Paging and Page Replacement » Copy-on-write and zero-fill
311.title: Copy-on-write and zero-fill

312.body:
What if there's no free frame (slides pp. 670–675)? Pick a victim page, write it out, and reuse its frame. That costs two disk transfers per fault, unless the victim hasn't changed since it was loaded. A modify (dirty) bit , set by the hardware on any write to the page, lets the OS skip writing back clean pages. Slide p. 673: swap the victim out, mark it invalid, swap the desired page in, reset the page table. Which victim? "We want the algorithm that gives us the lowest page-fault rate," evaluated by running it on a reference string of page numbers and counting faults (p. 676). The slides use 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 FIFO : evict the page that's been in memory longest. Optimal (OPT) : evict the page that won't be used for the longest time. Unbeatable, and impossible to implement (it needs the future), but it's the yardstick (p. 695). LRU (least recently used) : evict the page whose last use is oldest. Implemented with a timestamp per page, copied from the clock on every reference (p. 696). It approximates OPT by assuming the recent past predicts the near future. MRU , LFU , MFU : most recently used, least or most frequently used. "Neither [LFU nor MFU] are in common use. They are expensive [and] do not approximate the optimal case very well" (p. 698). src/code/sims/paging.ts implements FIFO, OPT, and LRU as interchangeable classes (Chapter 20a explains the design): $ tsc --target es2022 paging.ts && node paging.js
FIFO 3 frames: 9 faults 4 frames: 10 faults
OPT 3 frames: 7 faults 4 frames: 6 faults
LRU 3 frames: 10 faults 4 frames: 8 faults These match the slides: 9 faults for FIFO with 3 frames (p. 690), 6 for OPT with 4 (p. 695). Slide p. 692: FIFO with 3 frames, 9 faults; with 4 frames, 10. Look at FIFO: more frames, more faults . That's Belady's anomaly (p. 692). "If we had more frames, we'd have fewer page faults. Right?" Not with FIFO. OPT and LRU are stack algorithms : the set of pages in memory with n frames is always a subset of the set with n + 1, so adding frames can never hurt them. FIFO has no such property. Exam-style
LRU, 3 frames, on 7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4. Faults on 7, 0, 1 (cold), 2 (evict 7, least recently used), 0 hits, 3 (evict 1), 0 hits, 4 (evict 2). Total: 6 faults. Work it the way the slides do: a column per reference, the frames' contents underneath, an F where a fault occurs. The effective access time with demand paging is dominated by the fault rate p : EAT = (1 − p ) × memory access + p × fault service time. With 200 ns memory and an 8 ms fault, even p = 0.001 gives EAT ≈ 8.2 μs, a 40× slowdown. To keep the slowdown under 10%, faults must be rarer than about 1 in 400,000 accesses. Locality is what makes that possible.

312.title: Page replacement

313.body: How many frames does each process get (slides pp. 700–702)? Each needs a minimum (the IBM 370's MOVE instruction could touch 6 pages). Beyond that: equal allocation (103 frames, 5 processes: 20 each, 3 spare), proportional allocation (by process size), or priority allocation . Global replacement lets a faulting process take a frame from anyone; local replacement restricts it to its own frames (p. 703). Global is more efficient when it works, and risky when it doesn't.
313.breadcrumbs: Demand Paging and Page Replacement » Allocating frames
313.title: Allocating frames

314.body: When processes don't have enough frames, they fault constantly, each fault steals a frame another process needs, the disk queue grows, and CPU utilization collapses. The OS, seeing low utilization, admits more processes, which makes it worse. "This is thrashing: all paging and no doing" (slides pp. 704–707). The cure is to give each process the frames its current locality needs. The working-set model (pp. 709–712) estimates that: the working set is the set of pages referenced in the last Δ references (the working-set window). Too small a Δ misses part of the locality; too large spans several. If the sum of all working-set sizes D exceeds the available frames m , the OS suspends a process rather than letting everyone thrash. The working set also answers the question left open on slide p. 658, how the pager "guesses at which pages will be used": on swap-in, load the working set. Windows does a version of this with per-process working-set minimums and maximums, trimming working sets when free memory runs low (pp. 713–714).
314.breadcrumbs: Demand Paging and Page Replacement » Thrashing
314.title: Thrashing

315.title: The final challenge: demand paging in rObSen

316.body: Why must the CPU roll back the PC on a page fault, rather than just retrying the memory access? With 24 frames, global replacement, and ten copies of the counting program running round-robin, about how many frames does each need, and will the system thrash? Why is OPT impossible in general, yet rObSen's swapper effectively achieves it? Answers Because the fault surfaces as an exception that abandons the rest of the instruction, partway through, after the PC has already moved past the opcode and maybe part of the operand. The kernel handles the fault later (on the next tick), not inside the instruction. Rolling the PC back to the instruction's start means the whole instruction simply runs again, from scratch, once the page is present. Two each (page 0 for code, page 1 for the counter at $30), 20 frames in total, so all ten working sets fit in 24 frames: no thrashing. With thirteen copies (26 frames needed), RR would keep evicting pages that are about to be needed, and it would thrash. OPT needs to know the future reference string, which a general OS doesn't. But under round-robin, the future order in which processes run is known: it's the ready queue. The process just preempted is at the back, so it's the one needed furthest in the future, and that's the one rObSen's swapper evicts (Chapter 17).

317.body: TypeScript deep dive Three times in this book a piece of rObSen has been one algorithm chosen from a family: the CPU scheduler (RR, FCFS, priority), the disk-arm scheduler (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, …), and page replacement (FIFO, OPT, LRU). The slides keep saying the same thing about all of them: the policy "should be written as a separate module of the operating system, allowing it to be replaced" (p. 801); a VFS uses "encapsulation and polymorphism" so the kernel needn't know which file system it's talking to (p. 764). This chapter shows the TypeScript for that idea.

318.body:
Chapter 11a used interfaces to describe data . They can also describe behaviour : a set of methods any implementation must provide. interface ReplacementPolicy { readonly name: string; /** Choose which resident page to evict. `now` is the index into the reference string. */ victim(frames: number[], refs: number[], now: number, history: Map<number, number>): number;
} That's the whole contract for a page-replacement policy: it has a name, and given the resident pages, the reference string, the current position, and a record of when each page was last used, it chooses a page to evict.

32.body: "Mechanisms determine how to do something, policies decide what will be done" (slide p. 130). Separating them means you can change your mind about the policy without rewriting the mechanism. rObSen has a clean example of this separation. The mechanism for giving a process the CPU is Kernel.dispatchProcess: copy the PCB's registers into the CPU, mark the PCB running, reset the quantum counter. The policy for which process gets it is dequeueNextReadyProcess, which looks at _SchedulerMode ("RR", "FCFS", or "PRIORITY") and picks. setschedule fcfs changes the policy with one assignment; the dispatcher doesn't care. (Chapter 13 shows that the separation is a little too clean: the policy picks a process, but the mechanism around it still preempts on every quantum, so FCFS quietly behaves like round-robin.)

320.body:
function countFaults(refs: number[], frameCount: number, policy: ReplacementPolicy): number { const frames: number[] = []; const lastUsed = new Map<number, number>(); let faults = 0; refs.forEach((page, now) => { if (!frames.includes(page)) { faults++; if (frames.length === frameCount) { const v = policy.victim(frames, refs, now, lastUsed); frames.splice(frames.indexOf(v), 1); } frames.push(page); } lastUsed.set(page, now); }); return faults;
} countFaults takes any ReplacementPolicy. It never asks which one; it just calls policy.victim(…), and each object supplies its own behaviour. That's polymorphism , and it's what lets the driver loop at the bottom run all three: for (const policy of [new Fifo(), new Optimal(), new Lru()]) { … } To add a policy, write one more class. countFaults doesn't change. That's the strategy pattern : the varying part of an algorithm (the strategy) is pulled out behind an interface and passed in.

323.body: An interface can specify behaviour (methods), not just data. class X implements I asks the compiler to check that X fulfils I, at the class's definition. Code written against the interface works with every implementation: polymorphism. Use function types for stateless strategies; use classes implementing an interface when the strategy carries state or several operations.

Branch offsets are signed (two's complement) and relative to the address after the two-byte BNE: 00–7F go forward 0–127 bytes, 80–FF go back 128–1 bytes. To branch back to address target from a BNE at address b : offset = ( target − ( b + 2)) & 0xFF. System calls (FF): X Effect 01 Print the integer in Y (decimal) 02 Print the 00-terminated string starting at the address in Y The handout notes that SYS isn't a real 6502 instruction and that "in the OS simulations, the CPU object will generate a software interrupt when it sees the SYS op code (FF)." rObSen's CPU instead performs the call directly (Chapter 2); Appendix C's patch routes it through the kernel.

326.body: Z flag. The handout has only CPX set Z. rObSen also sets Z after LDA, LDX, LDY, ADC, and INC (real-6502 behaviour). 02: 8D 30 00 STA $0030

15: 00 BRK function disassemble(bytes: number[], stopAtFirstBrk = true): string[] { const lines: string[] = []; let pc = 0; while (pc < bytes.length) { const op = bytes[pc]; const info = OPCODES[op]; if (!info) { lines.push(`${hex(pc)}: ${hex(op)} .byte $${hex(op)}`); pc += 1; continue; } let raw = hex(op); let operand = ""; if (info.mode === "immediate") { raw += " " + hex(bytes[pc + 1]); operand = `#$${hex(bytes[pc + 1])}`; pc += 2; } else if (info.mode === "absolute") { const lo = bytes[pc + 1], hi = bytes[pc + 2]; raw += ` ${hex(lo)} ${hex(hi)}`; operand = `$${hex((hi << 8) | lo, 4)}`; // little-endian: low byte first pc += 3; } else if (info.mode === "relative") { const offset = bytes[pc + 1]; const signed = offset < 0x80 ? offset : offset - 0x100; // two's complement pc += 2; raw += " " + hex(offset); operand = `$${hex((pc + signed) & 0xff)} ; ${signed >= 0 ? "+" : ""}${signed}`; } else { pc += 1; } const start = pc - raw.split(" ").length; lines.push(`${hex(start)}: ${raw.padEnd(10)} ${info.mnemonic} ${operand}`.trimEnd()); if (stopAtFirstBrk && op === 0x00) break; } return lines;
}

328.body:
Count to n . The only instruction that increments is INC, which works on memory, and the only comparison is CPX, which compares X to memory. So: put the limit in X, the counter in memory. A9 00 8D 30 00 ; counter = 0
A2 05 ; X = 5
EE 30 00 ; loop: counter++
EC 30 00 ; Z = (counter == 5)
D0 F8 ; if not, back to loop Unconditional branch. There's no JMP, but BNE always branches when Z = 0. Force it with a comparison you know fails: compare X against a memory cell holding a different value. Under rObSen's Z behaviour, an LDA of a nonzero value also clears Z. Print a string. Store the bytes somewhere after the code, terminated with 00, then A0 <addr> A2 02 FF. Print a number. AC <addr lo> <addr hi> (load it into Y) then A2 01 FF. A classic mistake, made by the sample program under rObSen's input box, is to load the result into the accumulator and then print Y (Chapter 5).

33.body: The slides survey several ways to organize an OS (pp. 132–149): MS-DOS is monolithic and barely structured: "its interfaces and levels of functionality are not well separated." Traditional UNIX has two parts, system programs and a kernel that holds "everything below the system-call interface and above the physical hardware": the file system, CPU scheduling, memory management, all in one level. The layered approach stacks layers from hardware (layer 0) to user interface (layer N); each layer uses only the services of the layers beneath it. A microkernel moves as much as possible out of the kernel into user-space servers that talk by message passing (Mach, and through it Apple's Darwin). It is easier to extend and port, and more reliable, at the cost of messaging overhead. Slide p. 141: the layered approach, layer 0 (hardware) at the core. rObSen is a monolithic kernel with layered intentions . Everything, including the shell, runs as one program with one address space (JavaScript's global scope), so in the slides' terms it's closest to traditional UNIX, minus the separation of system programs. The files follow a layered plan, as the map shows. The calls don't always respect it: Call From layer To layer Should go through _StdOut.putText in Cpu.opSystemCall hardware console a system-call trap into the kernel _CurrentProcess = null in Shell.shellLoad shell kernel state a kernel function _krnDiskDriver.readBlock in Control.updateDiskPanel host UI OS driver (acceptable: it's a debugging view, like a hardware probe) _Kernel.krnTrap in MemoryAccessor hardware kernel (correct in spirit: hardware raising a fault into the OS) None of these break anything today. They are the kind of shortcut that makes a system harder to change later, which is precisely the argument for layering.

338.body: rObSen was written against TypeScript 5, under which it compiles cleanly. TypeScript 6 (and the native TypeScript 7 compiler) change two defaults that matter here: strict is on unless you turn it off, and declaring a namespace with the old module keyword is an error. Under those versions the unmodified project reports 147 errors (it still emits JavaScript, so it still runs). Two small changes restore a clean build: Replace module TSOS { with namespace TSOS { in the 18 files that use it (Chapter 1a explains why they mean the same thing). Add "strict": false to compilerOptions in tsconfig.json, or, better, keep strict mode on and work through the errors it reports; most are the implicit-any parameters and unchecked nulls described in Chapters 3a and 6a.

34.body:
"A virtual machine takes the layered approach to its logical conclusion. It treats hardware and the operating system kernel as though they were all hardware" (slide p. 156). The host creates "the illusion that a process has its own processor and (virtual) memory," and each guest gets a virtual copy of the computer. The slides then distinguish two techniques (p. 158): Emulation : used when the guest's CPU type differs from the host's. "Generally slowest method." When the guest's code isn't compiled to native code, this is interpretation . Virtualization : the guest OS is compiled for the same CPU the host runs on, and runs natively, with a virtual machine manager (VMM) mediating. Slide p. 160: a non-virtual machine versus a virtual machine.
Slide p. 163: "Your OS Architecture": 6502a op codes, source/os (TSOS), source/host, the web browser. So which is rObSen? Both, in different places, and seeing that is the key to understanding its architecture. User programs are emulated. A 6502a program is a list of bytes that Cpu.cycle reads one at a time and interprets with a switch. That is textbook emulation by interpretation: the guest instruction set (6502a) differs from the real machine's (whatever the JavaScript engine compiles to), and every guest instruction costs dozens of real ones. The operating system is not emulated at all. The kernel, drivers, shell, memory manager, and scheduler are TypeScript compiled to JavaScript, and they run directly on the browser's JavaScript engine, the same "hardware" the host runs on. The OS never executes a single 6502a instruction. That makes rObSen's structure unusual. A real OS runs on its CPU. rObSen's OS runs beside its CPU, on the real machine, and supervises the emulated CPU from outside, deciding when it may execute (isExecuting), feeding it registers (dispatchProcess), and reading its state back (Cpu.cycle copies registers into the PCB). The nearest real-world analogue is a hypervisor that runs guest applications rather than guest operating systems, which is roughly what Alan's "A LITTLE BIT like a hypervisor" comment is gesturing at. This explains several things that might otherwise look odd: Why the OS can call _CPU.pause() or set _CPU.PC directly: it isn't running on that CPU, so it can reach in and set its registers like a debugger would. Why an infinite loop in a user program can't freeze the OS: the OS gets control back every clock tick regardless of what the CPU is doing, because the clock is a JavaScript timer the CPU can't block. Why an infinite loop in the OS freezes everything, including the clock: the OS and the host share one JavaScript thread (Chapter 10).

All twenty programs are the same 6502a code with a different letter in the data area. Disassembled (the start of one): 00: A9 00 LDA #$00
02: 8D 7B 00 STA $007B
…
1B: EC 7A 00 CPX $007A
1E: D0 39 BNE $59
20: A0 7D LDY #$7D
22: A2 02 LDX #$02
24: FF SYS ; print the string at $7D (the program's letter)
25: AC 7B 00 LDY $007B
28: A2 01 LDX #$01
2A: FF SYS ; print a counter
… Each prints its letter and a counter in a loop, and finally "<letter>done" from $7F. With twenty of them and three partitions, seventeen live on disk at any moment, so nearly every context switch is a roll-out plus a roll-in. If the swapper or the dispatcher has a bug, ip4x finds it. 35.body: The rest of Chapter 2 covers performance tuning (top, Task Manager), debugging (log files, core dumps, crash dumps, Kernighan's Law, DTrace), and system boot (a bootstrap loader in firmware locates the kernel, loads it, and starts it). rObSen's debugging facilities are its host log and its live panels. Kernel.krnTrace writes to the host log whenever tracing is on (trace on|off), throttling the "Idle" messages to one in ten so the log doesn't drown the browser. Every log line records the OS clock (ticks since Start), the source (host, OS, scheduler), and the wall-clock time in milliseconds, which is enough to compute interrupt latency by hand. The comment in krnInterruptHandler mentions exactly that ("so we can compute Interrupt Latency by analyzing the log file later on"). The boot sequence is Chapter 6's subject.

36.body: Classify each of the following as policy or mechanism: the round-robin quantum (q 6); Swapper.rollOut; Kernel.selectSwapVictim; MemoryManager.allocate's choice of the first free partition. The slide asks "Why use APIs rather than system calls?" rObSen's user programs have no API layer at all; they execute FF directly. What would an API for 6502a programs even look like? In what sense is the 6502a CPU "hardware" and the browser also "hardware"? Which one does a user program believe it runs on? Answers The quantum is a policy parameter. rollOut is mechanism (it moves bytes). selectSwapVictim is policy (it decides who ). Choosing the first free partition is a policy (first fit) built into an allocation mechanism; you could separate them by passing a strategy in, as Chapter 20a does for page replacement. A library of 6502a subroutines (say, "print string at address") that programs would call with a jump-to-subroutine instruction. The 6502a subset has no JSR/RTS, so there's no way to call a subroutine and return, which is why there's no API layer. The CPU is hardware to the user program : it's the only machine a 6502a program can see. The browser is hardware to the OS and host : it's what their code runs on. Each layer's "hardware" is just the layer beneath it.

We start at the bottom: the code that pretends to be a computer's case, power switch, crystal oscillator, and keyboard controller. It lives in two files, host/control.ts and host/devices.ts. Both carry the same header comment, and it's worth taking literally: This (and other host/simulation scripts) is the only place that we should see "web" code, such as DOM manipulation and event handling, and so on. The host is the only layer that knows it's running in a web page. Everything above it is supposed to believe it's running on a machine.

It finds the canvas (the screen), bolts the vector-font routines onto its drawing context, clears the host log, and checks whether a Glados testing function was loaded by index.html. If so, it creates her. Nothing is running yet.
