(<HTMLButtonElement>document.getElementById("btnHaltOS")).disabled = false; (<HTMLButtonElement>document.getElementById("btnReset")).disabled = false; (<HTMLButtonElement>document.getElementById("btnStep")).disabled = false; (<HTMLButtonElement>document.getElementById("btnPause")).disabled = false; Control.setPaused(false); // .. set focus on the OS console display ... document.getElementById("display").focus(); // ... Create and initialize the CPU (because it's part of the hardware) ... _CPU = new Cpu(); // Note: We could simulate multi-core systems by instantiating more than one instance of the CPU here. _CPU.init(); // There's more to do, like dealing with scheduling and such, but this would be a start. Pretty cool. _Memory = new Memory(); _MemoryAccessor = new MemoryAccessor(_Memory); const segmentSize = Memory.SIZE / 3; _MemoryManager = new MemoryManager( _Memory, _MemoryAccessor, segmentSize, 3, ); _MemoryManager.reset(); _PidCounter = 0; _ProcessTable.clear(); _CurrentProcess = null; if (_ReadyQueue) { _ReadyQueue.clear(); } _SchedulerCounter = _SchedulerQuantum; _RunAllMode = false; _CpuCycleCount = 0; // ... then set the host clock pulse ... _hardwareClockID = setInterval( Devices.hostClockPulse, CPU_CLOCK_INTERVAL, ); // .. and call the OS Kernel Bootstrap routine. _Kernel = new Kernel(); _Kernel.krnBootstrap(); // _GLaDOS.afterStartup() will get called in there, if configured. } Read it as a hardware power-on sequence: Enable the other front-panel buttons. Create the CPU and reset its registers. (Alan's comment: you could create two CPUs here to simulate a multi-core machine. "There's more to do… but this would be a start. Pretty cool.") Create memory (768 bytes), the memory accessor that guards it, and a memory manager with three 256-byte segments. Strictly speaking the memory manager is OS software, not hardware; rObSen creates it here because it needs references to the memory objects, and the kernel doesn't exist yet. Reset bookkeeping: PID counter, process table, ready queue, quantum counter. Start the clock : setInterval(Devices.hostClockPulse, CPU_CLOCK_INTERVAL) calls hostClockPulse every 100 milliseconds, forever. 39.body:
public static hostClockPulse(): void { // Increment the hardware (host) clock. _OSclock++; // Call the kernel clock pulse event handler. _Kernel.krnOnCPUClockPulse(); } That's the whole clock. Every 100 ms the host increments the global _OSclock and hands control to the kernel's krnOnCPUClockPulse, which either handles one pending interrupt or lets the CPU execute one instruction (or idles). So rObSen's CPU runs at a blistering 10 Hz . Ten instructions per second is slow enough to watch, which is the point. Clock pulse ≠ timer
globals.ts warns: "The timer is different from hardware/host clock pulses. Don't confuse these." The clock is the heartbeat that makes the machine step: it is hardware, it never stops, and it doesn't interrupt anybody. The timer is a device that counts down and raises TIMER_IRQ when it reaches zero, so the OS can take the CPU back from a process that has used up its quantum (slide p. 56). In rObSen the timer is the _SchedulerCounter that Cpu.cycle decrements (Chapter 13). Many clock pulses make one timer interrupt. Notice the design choice hidden here. On a real machine, the CPU runs continuously and the interrupt controller interrupts it. In rObSen, the clock calls the kernel, and the kernel decides whether this tick is spent on an interrupt or on a CPU instruction. Interrupts are handled between instructions, never during one, which is also how real CPUs behave: they check for pending interrupts at instruction boundaries. The project spec requires this: "Only allow context switches after fully completed CPU instruction cycles."

public static hostEnableKeyboardInterrupt(): void { // Listen for key press (keydown, actually) events in the Document // and call the simulation processor, which will in turn call the // OS interrupt handler. document.addEventListener("keydown", Devices.hostOnKeypress, false); } public static hostDisableKeyboardInterrupt(): void { document.removeEventListener("keydown", Devices.hostOnKeypress, false); } public static hostOnKeypress(event): void { // The canvas element CAN receive focus if you give it a tab index, which we have. // Check that we are processing keystrokes only from the canvas's id (as set in index.html). if (event.target.id === "display") { event.preventDefault(); // Note the pressed key code in the params (Mozilla-specific). var params = new Array( event.which, event.shiftKey, event.ctrlKey || event.metaKey, ); // Enqueue this interrupt on the kernel interrupt queue so that it gets to the Interrupt handler. _KernelInterruptQueue.enqueue(new Interrupt(KEYBOARD_IRQ, params)); } } hostEnableKeyboardInterrupt subscribes to the browser's keydown events; hostDisableKeyboardInterrupt unsubscribes. Those are the kernel's "enable interrupts" and "disable interrupts" for the keyboard (Chapter 6). When a key goes down: It's ignored unless the canvas (id="display") has focus. Typing into the program-input textarea shouldn't type into the OS. preventDefault() stops the browser's own handling (so Backspace doesn't navigate back and Tab doesn't move focus). The key code, Shift state, and Ctrl-or-Command state become the parameters of a new Interrupt(KEYBOARD_IRQ, params), which goes on the kernel's interrupt queue. That's all the keyboard hardware does: it raises an interrupt with some data attached. It doesn't decide what the key means. Turning key code 65 into "a" or "A" is the keyboard driver 's job (Chapter 7), and that's OS software. event.which
event.which is a deprecated property of keyboard events; modern code uses event.key (a string like "a") or event.code (a physical key like "KeyA"). rObSen keeps the numeric codes on purpose: numeric scan codes are what a real keyboard controller delivers, and translating them is exactly the job a driver should have.

41.body: public static hostBtnHaltOS_click(btn): void { Control.hostLog("Emergency halt", "host"); Control.hostLog("Attempting Kernel shutdown.", "host"); // Call the OS shutdown routine. _Kernel.krnShutdown(); // Stop the interval that's simulating our clock pulse. clearInterval(_hardwareClockID); // TODO: Is there anything else we need to do here? } public static hostBtnPause_click(btn): void { if (!_CPU || !_Kernel) { return; } if (!Control.isPaused) { Control.setPaused(true); _CPU.pause(); Control.hostLog("Paused execution", "host"); } else { if (_CurrentProcess) { Control.setPaused(false); _CPU.resume(); Control.hostLog("Resume execution", "host"); } else { Control.setPaused(true); Control.hostLog("Resume ignored: no active process.", "host"); } } Control.hostUpdateDisplays(); } public static hostBtnStep_click(btn): void { if (!_CPU || !_Kernel) { return; } Control.setPaused(true); if (!_CurrentProcess) { Control.hostLog("Step ignored: no active process.", "host"); return; } _CPU.pause(); _Kernel.krnStep(); } public static hostBtnReset_click(btn): void { // The easiest and most thorough way to do this is to reload (not refresh) the document. (<HTMLButtonElement>document.getElementById("btnReset")).disabled = true; (<HTMLButtonElement>document.getElementById("btnStep")).disabled = true; (<HTMLButtonElement>document.getElementById("btnPause")).disabled = true; location.reload(); } Halt is the emergency stop: it asks the kernel to shut down, then kills the clock with clearInterval. After Halt the machine is dead; nothing ticks. Pause flips the CPU's isExecuting flag off (or back on). The clock keeps ticking, so the kernel still handles keyboard interrupts while the CPU is paused. You can still type. Step forces pause mode and calls Kernel.krnStep, which advances _OSclock by hand and does one unit of work: handle one interrupt if any are queued, otherwise execute one CPU instruction. It's a manual clock pulse. (Project Part Two requires single-step.) Reset reloads the page. That re-runs everything from hostInit, wiping memory and the CPU. It does not wipe the disk, because sessionStorage survives a reload (Chapter 15).

42.body:
The host log is the machine's console printer: public static hostLog(msg: string, source: string = "?"): void { // Note the OS CLOCK. var clock: number = _OSclock; // Note the REAL clock in milliseconds since January 1, 1970. var now: number = new Date().getTime(); // Build the log string. var str: string = "({ clock:" + clock + ", source:" + source + ", msg:" + msg + ", now:" + now + " })" + "\n"; // Update the log console. var taLog = <HTMLInputElement>document.getElementById("taHostLog"); taLog.value = str + taLog.value; // TODO in the future: Optionally update a log database or some streaming service. } Each entry looks like ({ clock:42, source:OS, msg:Handling IRQ~1, now:1760000000000 }): the simulated time, who said it, what they said, and the real time in milliseconds since 1970. New entries are prepended so the newest is at the top. hostUpdateDisplays repaints the CPU registers, the process table, the memory dump, and the disk view. The kernel calls it at the end of every clock pulse, so the panels refresh ten times a second. The memory dump is a neat example of the host formatting raw state for humans: private static updateMemoryPanel(): void { const memoryEl = document.getElementById("memory-dump"); if (!memoryEl || !_Memory) { return; } const bytes = _Memory.snapshot(); const rows: string[] = []; for (let address = 0; address < bytes.length; address += 16) { const chunk = bytes .slice(address, address + 16) .map((value) => Control.hex(value)) .join(" "); rows.push(`${Control.hex(address, 4)}: ${chunk}`); } memoryEl.textContent = rows.join("\n"); } private static hex(value: number, width: number = 2): string { const mask = width > 2 ? 0xffff : 0xff; const normalized = (value ?? 0) & mask; return normalized.toString(16).toUpperCase().padStart(width, "0"); } hex(value, width) masks the value to one or two bytes, converts it to base 16, upper-cases it, and left-pads with zeros. (padStart and template literals are covered in Chapter 15a.) In the code
updateDiskPanel also runs on every clock pulse. It reads all 256 disk blocks with readBlock, and each readBlock calls loadImage, which re-parses the entire JSON disk image from sessionStorage. That's 256 full JSON parses, ten times a second, even when nothing on the disk has changed. It's fast enough on a modern laptop not to notice, but it's the kind of thing a real OS avoids with a cache or a dirty flag.

43.body: The host is small, but it establishes three ideas that everything else relies on: There is a heartbeat. All progress in the system happens on clock ticks. Nothing in the OS runs "in the background"; it runs because the clock called it. Devices raise interrupts; they don't interpret them. The keyboard hardware says "key 65 went down, Shift was held." The meaning is the OS's business. The front panel is outside the OS. Halt, Pause, Step, and Reset reach into the machine from outside, the way the physical buttons on a 1970s minicomputer did. Slide p. 22, "Your OS – CLI," with a terminal from the era the front-panel metaphor comes from. (iP1)

44.body: If you changed CPU_CLOCK_INTERVAL to 10, what would change about the system, and what wouldn't? Why does hostOnKeypress check event.target.id === "display"? What would go wrong without it? While the CPU is paused, can GLaDOS still type commands? Why? Answers Everything would run ten times faster in real time: the CPU at 100 Hz, interrupts handled sooner. Nothing measured in cycles would change: the quantum is still 6 cycles, turnaround and wait times (measured in CPU cycles) come out identical. The panels would also try to repaint 100 times a second. Without it, keystrokes typed into the User Program Input textarea would also be sent to the OS as interrupts, and preventDefault() would stop them from reaching the textarea, so you couldn't paste or edit programs. Yes. Pausing only clears _CPU.isExecuting. The clock keeps calling the kernel, which keeps draining the interrupt queue. (GLaDOS actually goes even further: she calls krnInterruptHandler directly, bypassing the queue.)

47.body:
Here's the line that finds the screen: _Canvas = <HTMLCanvasElement>document.getElementById("display"); and here's one from later in the same file: const pauseButton = document.getElementById("btnPause") as HTMLButtonElement | null; Both are type assertions . document.getElementById is declared (in TypeScript's built-in DOM definitions) to return HTMLElement | null: some element, or nothing. The compiler can't know that the element with id="display" is a <canvas>, so without help it would refuse _Canvas.getContext("2d"), because plain HTMLElement has no getContext method. The assertion says: trust me, it's a canvas . The two spellings mean the same thing: Form Example Notes Angle brackets <HTMLCanvasElement>expr The original syntax. Can't be used in .tsx files, because it collides with JSX tags. as expr as HTMLCanvasElement The modern form. Works everywhere. Prefer it. The important thing about an assertion is that it is not a conversion and not a check . It produces no JavaScript at all. Compare the TypeScript and the compiled output: _Canvas = <HTMLCanvasElement>document.getElementById("display"); _Canvas = document.getElementById("display"); If you're wrong, nothing tells you until something fails at runtime. rObSen has a harmless example of a wrong assertion: var taLog = <HTMLInputElement>document.getElementById("taHostLog");
taLog.value = str + taLog.value; taHostLog is a <textarea>, so its real type is HTMLTextAreaElement, not HTMLInputElement (an <input>). The code works anyway because both types happen to have a value property. The compiler accepted the claim and didn't check it. The honest version is as HTMLTextAreaElement.

48.body: setPaused does it properly: public static setPaused(paused: boolean): void { Control.isPaused = paused; const pauseButton = document.getElementById("btnPause") as HTMLButtonElement | null; if (pauseButton) { pauseButton.textContent = paused ? "Resume" : "Pause"; } } as HTMLButtonElement | null keeps the possibility of null in the type, and the if (pauseButton) check then narrows the type to HTMLButtonElement inside the block. This is the shape to imitate: assert only what you're sure of (it's a button if it exists), and let a runtime check handle the rest. Chapter 6a covers narrowing in depth.

5.body: rObSen is really two programs sharing one browser tab. The host (source/host/) pretends to be hardware. It has a clock that ticks every 100 ms, a 768-byte memory, a memory accessor that sits between the CPU and memory, a 6502a-flavoured CPU, and a keyboard that raises interrupts. It is the only code allowed to touch the web page directly (the DOM), and it paints the panels you see beside the console. The client OS (source/os/) is the operating system proper. It has a kernel with an interrupt handler, device drivers for the keyboard and the disk, a console and a shell, process control blocks, a memory manager, a scheduler, and a swapper. The browser is the bare metal underneath both. Alan's comment at the top of control.ts puts it this way: the browser's document environment is "the 'bare metal' (so to speak) for which we write code that hosts our client OS," which makes the host "A LITTLE BIT like a hypervisor." Chapter 2 picks this analogy apart. CLIENT OS — source/os/ Shell (shell.ts) · Console (console.ts, canvastext.ts) CLI: parse → look up command → call it. Prompt, history, tab completion, aliases. Processes (pcb.ts) PCB per program; states New/Ready/ Running/Terminated Memory manager (memoryManager.ts) 3 fixed partitions of 256 bytes; allocate, load, release Scheduler + dispatcher (kernel.ts) RR / FCFS / PRIORITY; timer ISR; context switch via PCB save/restore Swapper (swapper.ts) roll-out / roll-in when the three partitions are full Kernel core (kernel.ts) · Drivers (deviceDriverKeyboard.ts, deviceDriverDisk.ts) bootstrap · interrupt queue · interrupt handler (switch on IRQ) · mode bit · trap/BSOD keyboard ISR → input queue · disk driver: track/sector/block file system in sessionStorage HOST "HARDWARE" — source/host/ Clock & devices setInterval → 100 ms keydown → KEYBOARD_IRQ CPU (cpu.ts) PC, IR, Acc, X, Y, Z fetch → decode → execute Memory + accessor Uint8Array(0x300), MAR/MDR logical → base + offset Control (control.ts): Start/Halt/Pause/Step/Reset · host log · live panels The browser: JavaScript engine, event loop, DOM, canvas, sessionStorage — the "bare metal" rObSen's layers. Blue is the operating system you wrote; amber is the simulated machine it runs on; grey is the real machine underneath both. Compare it with the slide Alan drew of the same thing: Slide p. 163, "Your OS Architecture" (Chapter 2). The iP1/iP2/iP3 flags mark which project iteration builds which piece.

50.body:
None of the DOM types (HTMLElement, HTMLCanvasElement, KeyboardEvent, Document) are defined in rObSen. They come from declaration files (.d.ts) that ship with the TypeScript compiler and describe the browser's built-in APIs. A declaration file contains types but no code, for example: interface HTMLCanvasElement extends HTMLElement { height: number; width: number; getContext(contextId: "2d", options?: CanvasRenderingContext2DSettings): CanvasRenderingContext2D | null; // …
} The compiler includes these definitions automatically, based on the target in tsconfig.json. That's how it knows setInterval returns a number in browsers, how event.preventDefault() is spelled, and that sessionStorage.getItem returns string | null. (When you need types for a library that doesn't ship its own, you install a @types/… package, which is the same idea.)

The next layer up is memory, and the piece of hardware that stands between the CPU and memory. This chapter is about the hardware half of memory management. The software half, the memory manager that decides which process gets which partition, waits for Chapter 11.

55.body:
namespace TSOS { export class Memory { // Memory Design inspired by LongOS on the Hall of Fame public static SIZE = 0x300; private bytes: Uint8Array; public mar: number; public mdr: number; constructor(size: number = Memory.SIZE) { this.bytes = new Uint8Array(size); this.mar = 0; } public size(): number { return this.bytes.length; } public read(address: number): number { this.validateAddress(address); this.mar = address; this.mdr = this.bytes[address]; return this.mdr; } public write(address: number, value: number) { this.validateAddress(address); const normalized = value & 0xff; this.mar = address; this.mdr = normalized; this.bytes[address] = normalized; } public clear(): void { this.bytes.fill(0x00); this.mar = 0; this.mdr = 0; } public snapshot(): number[] { return Array.from(this.bytes); } //function was suggested by ChatGPT private validateAddress(address: number) { const isInteger = Number.isInteger(address); if (!isInteger || address < 0 || address >= this.bytes.length) { throw new Error(`Memory access out of bounds at address ${address}`); } } }
} That's the whole of RAM. A few details: Size. 0x300 is hexadecimal for 768: three blocks of 0x100 (256) bytes. The Chapter 8 slides say it directly: "768 bytes will do for us, eventually. 256 for iP2." Project Part Two needs one 256-byte program; Part Three needs three at once. Lab 011 is the moment you make the jump: "Increase your memory from 256 bytes to 768 bytes. … Be sure that you can map a memory partition number (0,1,2) to the appropriate base address (0, 256, 512)." Uint8Array. A typed array of unsigned 8-bit integers. Every element is a byte, 0 to 255, and the array is created full of zeros. If you store 256 into a Uint8Array, it silently wraps to 0; store -1 and you get 255. write masks with value & 0xff anyway, which makes the intent explicit and also keeps mdr (which is an ordinary number) honest. Chapter 5a explains & 0xff. MAR and MDR. The memory address register holds the address being accessed, and the memory data register holds the byte being read or written. Real memory hardware works through exactly these two registers: the CPU puts an address in the MAR, and the byte appears in (or is taken from) the MDR. rObSen's read and write update them on every access even though nothing else reads them. They're there to model the hardware faithfully, and you could display them in the CPU panel to watch memory traffic. Bounds checking. validateAddress throws a JavaScript Error if the address isn't an integer in range. A comment credits ChatGPT with the function, and another credits LongOS (a 2024 Hall of Fame project) with the overall design. Throwing is the hardware equivalent of a bus error : an access to an address where no memory exists.

56.body: If the CPU read _Memory directly, every program would have to know where in physical memory it had been loaded. A program loaded at 0x0100 would need every address in its code adjusted by 256. That's compile-time binding (slide p. 559), and it's what MS-DOS .com files did: the program only works at one location. Instead, programs are written as if they start at address 0x0000, and something between the CPU and memory adds the right offset on every access. The slides call that something the MMU (memory-management unit), with a relocation register holding the offset: Slide p. 563: the CPU issues logical address 346; the relocation register adds 14000; memory sees physical address 14346. Alan's annotation: "it's really the hardware Memory Accessor (MA), not the software MMU." The annotation matters. In the course's vocabulary, the memory accessor (MA) is the hardware that translates addresses on every access, and the memory manager (MMU) is the OS software that decides where each process lives. The textbook blurs the two; the course separates them because rObSen does. Slide p. 572 explains why the translation has to be done in rObSen's memory accessor rather than a register: "our hardware/host simulation does not support a Relocation Register (because the 6502 did not have one)."
56.breadcrumbs: Memory and the Memory Accessor » Why a memory accessor ?
56.title: Why a memory accessor ?

57.body:
module TSOS { export class MemoryAccessor { constructor(private readonly memory: Memory) {} public read(address: number): number { const translated = this.translateAddress(address, "read"); return this.memory.read(translated); } public write(address: number, value: number): void { const translated = this.translateAddress(address, "write"); this.memory.write(translated, value); } public loadBytes(startAddress: number, bytes: number[]): void { this.validateRange(startAddress, bytes.length); for (let offset = 0; offset < bytes.length; offset++) { this.write(startAddress + offset, bytes[offset]); } } public clear(): void { this.memory.clear(); } private validateRange(startAddress: number, length: number): void { if (length === 0) { return; } const endAddress = startAddress + length - 1; if (startAddress < 0 || endAddress >= this.memory.size()) { throw new Error( `Memory range ${startAddress.toString(16)}-${endAddress.toString(16)} exceeds physical memory`, ); } this.translateAddress(startAddress, "load"); this.translateAddress(endAddress, "load"); } private translateAddress(address: number, operation: string): number { const isExecuting = _CPU && _CPU.isExecuting; if (!isExecuting || !_CurrentProcess) { return address; } const logical = address & 0xff; const physical = _CurrentProcess.base + logical; if (!_CurrentProcess.contains(physical)) { const message = `Memory ${operation} at 0x${physical .toString(16) .padStart(4, "0")} violates base/limit for PID ${_CurrentProcess.pid}`; this.handleMemoryViolation(message); } return physical; } private handleMemoryViolation(message: string): void { if (_CurrentProcess) { _CurrentProcess.markTerminated(); } if (_CPU) { _CPU.pause(); } if (_Kernel && typeof _Kernel.krnTrap === "function") { _Kernel.krnTrap(message); } else { throw new Error(message); } } }
}

59.body:
Look at the arithmetic again. logical is address & 0xff, so it's always between 0 and 255. Every partition is exactly 256 bytes, so limit = base + 255. Therefore physical = base + logical is always between base and base + 255, which is always inside [base, limit]. The violation branch is unreachable . That doesn't mean programs can escape their partitions. It means they can't escape, but not for the reason the code suggests. Masking with & 0xff folds every address into the process's own 256 bytes. A program that tries to store to 0x01FF, which in physical terms is the last byte of partition 1, actually stores to logical 0xFF of its own partition. You can verify it: load A9 07 8D FF 01 00 (load 7 into the accumulator, store it at $01FF, break) and run it in partition 0. It completes normally, with no trap, and byte 0x00FF of partition 0 becomes 7. In the code
Protection is enforced by wraparound, silently, not by trapping. That's a defensible design (it's roughly what a 256-byte segment register with no limit check would do), but it contradicts the project spec, which asks the OS to handle "memory out of bounds or access violation attempts," because the violation is never even noticed. A program with a bad address corrupts its own data instead of being stopped. To actually detect violations, check the untranslated address before masking: if address > 0xff (or more generally address >= limit - base + 1), it's outside the process's logical address space. Appendix C has the patch. In the code
If a violation were detected, handleMemoryViolation calls krnTrap, which paints the Blue Screen of Death and shuts down the whole OS. A protection fault in one user process should kill that process and let the others carry on. Shutting down the kernel because a user program misbehaved is the opposite of what protection is for. The same is true of invalid opcodes (Chapter 5).

61.body: One commit message from November 9 reads: "fixed the segmentation bug uncovered by GLaDOS: PCBs now store logical (0–255) PCs." Before that fix, a PCB saved a physical program counter. When the dispatcher restored it into the CPU and the accessor translated it again, base got added twice, and a process in partition 1 or 2 jumped into the wrong memory. Now Cpu.cycle saves this.PC & 0xff into the PCB, so PCs are always logical. The rule this enforces is worth remembering: everything the process can see is logical; only the accessor knows physical.

62.body: Memory is a 768-byte Uint8Array with MAR/MDR and a bounds check. MemoryAccessor translates logical addresses (0–255) to physical ones by adding the running process's base. It's rObSen's stand-in for a relocation register. The OS bypasses translation by working while the CPU isn't executing. Protection works by masking, so out-of-range addresses wrap silently, and the explicit violation check is dead code.

63.body: A process in partition 2 executes AD 10 00 (load the accumulator from $0010). Which physical address is read? Why does translateAddress check _CPU.isExecuting rather than _Mode? Write the one-line condition that would make the violation check meaningful. Answers Base of partition 2 is 0x0200, so physical 0x0210. Because _Mode doesn't reliably reflect whether a user program is running: the kernel sets it to "user" at the end of many kernel functions even when no process is running. isExecuting is the CPU's own state, so it's the better signal. (A cleaner design would make the CPU set the mode bit when it starts and stops executing user code, and have the accessor read that.) Before masking: if (address < 0 || address > _CurrentProcess.limit - _CurrentProcess.base) handleMemoryViolation(…).

65.body:
The long way to write a class declares fields, then assigns them in the constructor: class Memory { public static SIZE = 0x300; // static field with an initializer private bytes: Uint8Array; // instance field, assigned in the constructor public mar: number; public mdr: number; // never assigned in the constructor! constructor(size: number = Memory.SIZE) { this.bytes = new Uint8Array(size); this.mar = 0; }
} That's memory.ts, nearly verbatim. Three details: Default parameter values. size: number = Memory.SIZE means "if the caller passes nothing (or undefined), use 768." Defaults are evaluated at call time, so they can refer to other things that exist by then, such as a static field. Static fields like SIZE live on the class (Memory.SIZE), not on instances. See Chapter 3a. mdr is never initialized in the constructor, so it starts as undefined until the first read or write. Under strict mode (specifically strictPropertyInitialization), TypeScript would flag that line: "Property 'mdr' has no initializer and is not definitely assigned in the constructor." rObSen's tsconfig.json doesn't mention strict, so under TypeScript 5 (strict off by default) it compiles; TypeScript 6 and later default to strict and report exactly that error. The fix is a one-word initializer, public mdr = 0;.

Modifier Who can use it public (the default) anyone protected the class and its subclasses private only the class itself Memory.validateAddress is private: the outside world calls read and write, and the bounds check is an internal detail. MemoryAccessor.translateAddress is private too. The kernel never asks the accessor "what would this address translate to?"; it just reads and writes. These modifiers are compile-time only . They vanish from the JavaScript, so a determined caller can still write (_MemoryAccessor as any).translateAddress(5, "x"). JavaScript has its own, runtime-enforced privacy, spelled with a #: class Memory { #bytes = new Uint8Array(0x300); // truly private, even at runtime
} rObSen doesn't use # fields. For a teaching OS where you sometimes want to poke at internals from the browser console, compile-time privacy is arguably the friendlier choice.

68.body: readonly means "assigned once, in the declaration or the constructor, never again." MemoryAccessor's memory is readonly because the accessor is wired to one physical memory for life. PCB.pid is readonly because a process's identity never changes. MemoryManager.partitions is readonly too, but notice that this only freezes the reference : the code still changes partition.allocated and partition.pid inside the array. readonly is shallow. To freeze contents as well, you'd use ReadonlyArray<MemoryPartition> and Readonly<MemoryPartition>, or Object.freeze at runtime. Like the access modifiers, readonly is erased at compile time.

7.body: Most of the book is about these three paths. Keep them in mind; every chapter adds detail to one of them. A keystroke. You press v. The browser fires a keydown event. Devices.hostOnKeypress (host) wraps the key code in an Interrupt(KEYBOARD_IRQ, …) and puts it on the kernel interrupt queue. On the next clock pulse, Kernel.krnOnCPUClockPulse sees a pending interrupt and calls krnInterruptHandler, which switches to kernel mode and calls the keyboard driver's ISR. The driver turns key code 86 into the character "v" and puts it on the kernel input queue. Console.handleInput drains that queue, draws the v on the canvas, and appends it to its line buffer. When you press Enter, the console hands the buffer to Shell.handleInput. (Chapters 3, 6, 7, 8.) A program. You paste hex into the User Program Input box and type load. The shell validates the hex, asks the memory manager for a free 256-byte partition, copies the bytes in, builds a PCB, and puts it on the ready queue. run 0 (or runall) asks the kernel to dispatch it: the PCB's saved registers are copied into the CPU and isExecuting flips to true. From then on, each clock pulse with no pending interrupt runs exactly one instruction. When the instruction is 00 (BRK), the kernel retires the process and frees its partition. (Chapters 4, 5, 9, 11.) A context switch. With several programs loaded and runall running, the CPU counts down a quantum (6 cycles by default). At zero it enqueues a TIMER_IRQ. The timer ISR puts the current PCB at the back of the ready queue, picks the next one, swaps it in from "disk" if it isn't in memory, and dispatches it. (Chapters 12, 13, 17.)

71.body: BrowserHost: clock & devicesHost: memoryHost: CPUKernelDriversConsole & shellProcessesMemory managerSchedulerFile systemSwapper Slides: Chapter 1, pp. 23–28 (CPU and registers); Chapter 3, pp. 175–177 (registers in the PCB); Chapter 8, p. 556 (6502a op codes). Reference: Alan's "6502alan" instruction-set handout. The last piece of hardware is the processor. rObSen's CPU is a tiny interpreter for a 14-instruction subset of the MOS 6502, the chip inside the Apple II, the Commodore 64, and the original Nintendo. In 296 lines it implements the instruction cycle that every CPU performs: fetch an instruction from memory, decode it, execute it, repeat.

72.body: export class Cpu { constructor( public PC: number = 0, public Acc: number = 0, public Xreg: number = 0, public Yreg: number = 0, public Zflag: number = 0, public isExecuting: boolean = false, public IR: number = 0, ) {} Register Width Purpose PC (program counter) 8 bits in practice Logical address of the next byte to fetch IR (instruction register) 8 bits The opcode currently being executed Acc (accumulator) 8 bits The arithmetic register: loads, stores, adds Xreg, Yreg 8 bits Index registers; also the system-call selector (X) and argument (Y) Zflag 1 bit Zero flag: set by comparisons, tested by branches isExecuting 1 bit Not a real 6502 register: "is the CPU running user code right now?" These are the "CPU registers" that slide p. 175 says belong in a process control block, and exactly the set that Project Part Two asks you to "update and display" in real time alongside memory and the PCB.

73.body: Every clock pulse that isn't spent on an interrupt calls cycle(): public cycle(): void { if (!this.isExecuting) { return; } if (!_CurrentProcess) { this.isExecuting = false; return; } _Kernel.krnTrace("CPU cycle"); _CpuCycleCount++; const opcode = this.fetchByte(); this.IR = opcode; _CurrentProcess.ir = opcode; switch (opcode) { case 0xa9: this.opLoadAccImmediate(); break; case 0xad: this.opLoadAccAbsolute(); break; case 0x8d: this.opStoreAccAbsolute(); break; case 0x6d: this.opAddWithCarry(); break; case 0xa2: this.opLoadXImmediate(); break; case 0xae: this.opLoadXAbsolute(); break; case 0xa0: this.opLoadYImmediate(); break; case 0xac: this.opLoadYAbsolute(); break; case 0xea: this.opNoOperation(); break; case 0xec: this.opCompareX(); break; case 0xee: this.opIncrementAbsolute(); break; case 0xd0: this.opBranchNotEqual(); break; case 0x00: this.opBreak(); break; case 0xff: this.opSystemCall(); break; default: this.opInvalid(opcode); break; } if (_CurrentProcess) { _CurrentProcess.pc = this.PC & 0xff; _CurrentProcess.acc = this.Acc & 0xff; _CurrentProcess.xReg = this.Xreg & 0xff; _CurrentProcess.yReg = this.Yreg & 0xff; _CurrentProcess.zFlag = this.Zflag & 0xff; _CurrentProcess.ir = this.IR & 0xff; } if (_CurrentProcess && this.isExecuting) { if (_SchedulerCounter > 0) { _SchedulerCounter--; } if (_SchedulerCounter <= 0) { _KernelInterruptQueue.enqueue(new Interrupt(TIMER_IRQ, [])); _SchedulerCounter = 0; } _CurrentProcess.quantumRemaining = Math.max(_SchedulerCounter, 0); _CurrentProcess.turnaroundCycles = _CpuCycleCount - _CurrentProcess.arrivalCycle; } } Five phases, in order: Guard. Do nothing unless the CPU is executing and there's a current process. This is what Pause turns off. Fetch. fetchByte() reads the byte at PC through the memory accessor and advances PC. That byte goes into IR. Decode. The switch maps the opcode to a handler. An unknown opcode goes to opInvalid. Execute. The handler fetches any operand bytes it needs (advancing PC again), does its work, and updates registers and memory. Write back and tick. The registers are copied into the running PCB (always masked to 8 bits, and always logical ; see the GLaDOS bug in Chapter 4), and the scheduler's countdown is decremented. When the countdown reaches zero, the CPU enqueues a TIMER_IRQ. That is the timer hardware from slide p. 56, built into the CPU (Chapter 13). Note that cycle executes exactly one instruction , however many bytes it occupies. The 6502 spends several clock cycles on a three-byte instruction; rObSen's CPU spends one. That's a simplification, and a convenient one: "turnaround time in CPU cycles" becomes "turnaround time in instructions."

73.title: The instruction cycle

74.body: The 6502a subset uses four addressing modes: Mode Bytes Example Meaning Implied 1 EA (NOP), 00 (BRK), FF (SYS) No operand Immediate 2 A9 05 (LDA #$05) The operand is the value Absolute 3 AD 50 00 (LDA $0050) The operand is a memory address Relative 2 D0 EF (BNE −17) The operand is a signed offset from PC private fetchByte(): number { this.ensureOperandAvailable(1); const value = _MemoryAccessor.read(this.PC & 0xff); this.PC = (this.PC + 1) & 0xff; return value & 0xff; } private fetchWord(): number { this.ensureOperandAvailable(2); const low = _MemoryAccessor.read(this.PC & 0xff); const high = _MemoryAccessor.read((this.PC + 1) & 0xff); this.PC = (this.PC + 2) & 0xff; return ((high << 8) | low) & 0xffff; } Little-endian addresses. An absolute address is two bytes, low byte first . The bytes 50 00 mean address $0050, not $5000. fetchWord reads the low byte, then the high byte, and assembles (high << 8) | low: shift the high byte left 8 bits and combine. (Chapter 5a explains <<, |, and &.) This is why every 6502a program is full of 00s: the high byte of every address in a 256-byte program is zero. PC wraparound. this.PC = (this.PC + 1) & 0xff keeps the program counter in the range 0–255. The spec says "the program counter for any process should never be greater than FF (255)," and this is how rObSen enforces it: increment past FF and you're back at 00. Missing operands. ensureOperandAvailable checks, before reading, that the bytes an instruction needs fit inside the process's partition. If AD is the last byte of the partition, there's nowhere to get its address from, and the CPU traps with "Missing operand for opcode…". The spec asks for "missing operands (if you can detect that)" to be handled. In practice, MemoryManager.load pads every partition with zeros, so an operand is almost always "available" (as 00), and the check only fires at the very end of a partition.

74.title: Operands and addressing modes

75.body:
Here's every handler. Each is a few lines; the interesting ones get commentary afterwards. private opLoadAccImmediate(): void { this.Acc = this.fetchByte(); this.updateZeroFlag(this.Acc); } private opLoadAccAbsolute(): void { const address = this.fetchWord(); this.Acc = this.readMemory(address); this.updateZeroFlag(this.Acc); } private opStoreAccAbsolute(): void { const address = this.fetchWord(); this.writeMemory(address, this.Acc); } private opAddWithCarry(): void { const address = this.fetchWord(); const value = this.readMemory(address); this.Acc = (this.Acc + value) & 0xff; this.updateZeroFlag(this.Acc); } private opLoadXImmediate(): void { this.Xreg = this.fetchByte(); this.updateZeroFlag(this.Xreg); } private opLoadXAbsolute(): void { const address = this.fetchWord(); this.Xreg = this.readMemory(address); this.updateZeroFlag(this.Xreg); } private opLoadYImmediate(): void { this.Yreg = this.fetchByte(); this.updateZeroFlag(this.Yreg); } private opLoadYAbsolute(): void { const address = this.fetchWord(); this.Yreg = this.readMemory(address); this.updateZeroFlag(this.Yreg); } private opNoOperation(): void { // Intentionally empty. } private opCompareX(): void { const address = this.fetchWord(); const value = this.readMemory(address); this.Zflag = this.Xreg === value ? 1 : 0; } private opIncrementAbsolute(): void { const address = this.fetchWord(); const value = (this.readMemory(address) + 1) & 0xff; this.writeMemory(address, value); this.updateZeroFlag(value); } private opBranchNotEqual(): void { const offset = this.fetchByte(); if (this.Zflag !== 0) { return; } const signedOffset = offset < 0x80 ? offset : offset - 0x100; this.PC = (this.PC + signedOffset) & 0xff; } ADC (6D) adds a memory byte to the accumulator and masks to 8 bits. The real 6502 also adds the carry flag and sets it on overflow ("add with carry"); the 6502a subset has no carry flag, so 250 + 10 quietly becomes 4. CPX (EC) compares X to a memory byte and sets Zflag to 1 if they're equal, 0 if not. It is the only way to make a decision, because… BNE (D0) is the only branch: "Branch n bytes if Z flag = 0." The operand is a signed byte in two's complement: 00–7F mean 0 to +127, 80–FF mean −128 to −1. So D0 EF jumps back 17 bytes (0xEF − 0x100 = −17). The offset is relative to the PC after the two-byte branch instruction has been fetched, which is the trap everyone falls into when hand-assembling: at $20, D0 EF lands at $22 − 17 = $11. INC (EE) increments a byte in memory in place, the only read-modify-write instruction. BRK (00) stops the CPU and tells the kernel the process is done (krnCompleteCurrentProcess). The handout calls it a "system call," and functionally it's the exit() system call. Because memory is zero-filled, running off the end of a program into unused memory executes 00 and exits cleanly, which is convenient and occasionally hides bugs. SYS (FF) is covered in Chapter 2: X = 1 prints the integer in Y; X = 2 prints the zero-terminated string at address Y. In the code
The Z flag is set more often than the spec allows. The instruction-set handout says only CPX sets Z ("Sets the Z (zero) flag if equal"), and only BNE reads it. rObSen's CPU also sets Z after LDA, LDX, LDY, ADC, and INC (updateZeroFlag), which is what a real 6502 does, but not what the 6502a spec says. Most test programs put CPX immediately before BNE, so the difference rarely shows. Here's one where it does:
A9 00 D0 02 A0 01 A2 01 FF 00
LDA #0 · BNE +2 · LDY #1 · LDX #1 · SYS · BRK
Under the spec, Z is still 0 when BNE executes (nothing has set it), so the branch skips LDY #1 and the program prints 0. Under rObSen, LDA #0 sets Z to 1, the branch falls through, and it prints 1. (Checked by running rObSen's compiled code.) If your goal is to match the class's reference emulator and test programs, remove the updateZeroFlag calls from everything except CPX. In the code
An invalid opcode kills the whole OS. opInvalid marks the process terminated and calls krnTrap, which shows the BSOD and shuts the kernel down. Load A9 01 FE 00 and run it: Blue Screen, and you must press Reset. A bad instruction in a user program is the user program's problem; the OS should kill that process (releasing its partition and removing it from the ready queue, which markTerminated alone doesn't do) and carry on with the others. Appendix C shows a fix that routes it through krnKillProcess instead.

76.body:
Being able to trace 6502a by hand is the skill this chapter exists to build. Here's the sample program printed under the input box in index.html, disassembled by src/code/sims/disasm.ts: 00: A9 05 LDA #$05
02: 8D 50 00 STA $0050 ; five = 5
05: A9 00 LDA #$00
07: 8D 51 00 STA $0051 ; i = 0
0A: A2 05 LDX #$05 ; X = 5 (loop limit)
0C: A9 00 LDA #$00
0E: 8D 60 00 STA $0060 ; sum = 0
11: AD 60 00 LDA $0060 ; loop1: Acc = sum
14: 6D 50 00 ADC $0050 ; Acc += five
17: 8D 60 00 STA $0060 ; sum = Acc
1A: EE 51 00 INC $0051 ; i++
1D: EC 51 00 CPX $0051 ; Z = (X == i)
20: D0 EF BNE $11 ; if not equal, loop
22: A9 00 LDA #$00
24: 8D 51 00 STA $0051 ; i = 0
27: A9 00 LDA #$00
29: 8D 61 00 STA $0061 ; prod = 0
2C: AD 61 00 LDA $0061 ; loop2: prod += sum, five times
2F: 6D 60 00 ADC $0060
32: 8D 61 00 STA $0061
35: EE 51 00 INC $0051
38: EC 51 00 CPX $0051
3B: D0 EF BNE $2C
3D: AD 61 00 LDA $0061 ; Acc = prod
40: A2 01 LDX #$01 ; syscall 1: print integer in Y
42: FF SYS
43: 00 BRK The first loop computes 5 × 5 = 25 by repeated addition; the second computes 25 × 5 = 125. Total: 75 instructions (7 + 6×5 + 4 + 6×5 + 4), so 7.5 seconds at 10 Hz. The variables live at $50, $51, $60, $61, inside the program's own 256 bytes, after the code. And the output? It prints 0 , then the kernel reports ACC = 125. The program loads the product into the accumulator , but system call 1 prints the Y register , which was never set. A one-byte change fixes it: AC 61 00 (LDY $0061) instead of AD 61 00. This is a nice reminder that the CPU does what the bytes say, not what the programmer meant. A second example, exercising both system calls: 00: A9 41 LDA #$41 ; 'A'
02: 8D 10 00 STA $0010 ; store it just past the code
05: A0 10 LDY #$10 ; Y = address of the string
07: A2 02 LDX #$02 ; syscall 2: print string at Y
09: FF SYS ; prints "A" (byte $11 is 00, which ends the string)
0A: A2 01 LDX #$01
0C: A0 07 LDY #$07
0E: FF SYS ; prints "7"
0F: 00 BRK Output: A7. Exam-style
Hand-assemble: "count X from 0 up to 3, then print it." You need a memory cell for the counter (say $40), because the only register you can increment is a memory byte, and the only comparison is X against memory.
A9 00 8D 40 00 ; $40 = 0
A2 03 ; X = 3
EE 40 00 ; loop: $40++ (address 07)
EC 40 00 ; Z = (X == $40)
D0 F8 ; BNE loop: after this instruction PC = $0F; $0F - 8 = $07
AC 40 00 ; Y = $40
A2 01 FF 00 ; print Y, exit
It prints 3. Check the branch offset: the BNE sits at $0D, so after fetching it the PC is $0F; we want $07; $07 - $0F = -8 = $F8.

77.body: public pause(): void { this.isExecuting = false; } public resume(): void { if (_CurrentProcess) { this.isExecuting = true; } } public step(resumeAfter: boolean = false): void { if (!_CurrentProcess) { return; } const wasExecuting = this.isExecuting; this.isExecuting = true; this.cycle(); if (resumeAfter && wasExecuting && _CurrentProcess) { this.isExecuting = true; } else { this.isExecuting = false; } } step runs exactly one cycle even when the CPU is paused, by temporarily setting isExecuting. That's the mechanism behind the Step button (Chapter 3), which the spec requires.

77.title: Single-stepping

78.body: The CPU holds PC, IR, Acc, X, Y, and Z, and executes one instruction per call to cycle. Absolute addresses are little-endian; branch offsets are signed and relative to the following instruction. After each instruction the registers are saved to the PCB and the scheduler's countdown ticks. Two deviations from the spec: Z is set by loads and arithmetic, and invalid instructions crash the OS rather than the process.

8.body:
Lab 000
Lab 000 asks you to put the project in a private GitHub repository, add Alan as a collaborator, record the Part One requirements as GitHub Issues, and set up your development environment. What follows is the environment part. rObSen has no bundler. The TypeScript compiler turns each .ts file in source/ into a .js file in distrib/, and index.html loads those files with plain <script> tags. The configuration is all in tsconfig.json: { "compilerOptions": { "target" : "ES2023", "rootDir" : "source", "outDir" : "distrib", "sourceMap" : true, "extendedDiagnostics" : true }, "include": [ "source/**/*" ],
} So the whole build is: $ cd OS-Fall2025
$ tsc # reads tsconfig.json, writes distrib/**/*.js and .js.map Then open index.html in a browser and click Start . Which TypeScript?
rObSen was built with TypeScript 5, and tsc 5.9 compiles it with zero errors. TypeScript 6 and the native TypeScript 7 compiler change two defaults (strict mode on; the old module keyword for namespaces is an error), so with a current compiler the same command reports 147 errors. It still writes the JavaScript, and the OS still runs, but the noise hides real problems. Either install TypeScript 5 for this project (npm install --save-dev typescript@5 and run npx tsc), or make the two small changes in Appendix C. (`package.json` lists `gulp` as a dependency, a leftover from the original template. You don't need it.) Two things about this setup matter later. First, the order of the <script> tags in index.html is load-bearing: globals.js must come first, and kernel.js is deliberately last among the OS files. Second, because nothing is imported or exported between files in the module sense, every file shares one global scope. The first deep dive explains why that works, and what it costs. <!-- Globals CONSTANTS and _Variables. Must be included first. --> <script type="text/javascript" src="distrib/globals.js"></script> <!-- Host (Virtual Machine / Hardware Simulation) Routines --> <script type="text/javascript" src="distrib/host/control.js"></script> <script type="text/javascript" src="distrib/host/devices.js"></script> <script type="text/javascript" src="distrib/host/memory.js"></script> <script type="text/javascript" src="distrib/host/memoryAccessor.js" ></script> <script type="text/javascript" src="distrib/host/cpu.js"></script> <!-- Virtual OS Routines: Make sure Kernel code is last, since it needs those above it. --> <script type="text/javascript" src="distrib/os/interrupt.js"></script> <script type="text/javascript" src="distrib/os/canvastext.js"></script> <script type="text/javascript" src="distrib/os/console.js"></script> <script type="text/javascript" src="distrib/os/memoryManager.js" ></script> <script type="text/javascript" src="distrib/os/deviceDriver.js" ></script> <script type="text/javascript" src="distrib/os/deviceDriverDisk.js" ></script> <script type="text/javascript" src="distrib/os/deviceDriverKeyboard.js" ></script> <script type="text/javascript" src="distrib/os/swapper.js"></script> <script type="text/javascript" src="distrib/os/pcb.js"></script> <script type="text/javascript" src="distrib/os/queue.js"></script> <script type="text/javascript" src="distrib/os/shell.js"></script> <script type="text/javascript" src="distrib/os/shellCommand.js" ></script> <script type="text/javascript" src="distrib/os/userCommand.js"></script> <script type="text/javascript" src="distrib/os/kernel.js"></script> <!-- Other Routines --> <script type="text/javascript" src="distrib/utils.js"></script> <!-- Uncomment the line below to enable GLaDOS testing. --> <script src="test/glados-ip4x.js"></script> Note the last <script> line: glados-ip4x.js is enabled, so every time you load the page, GLaDOS (Alan's automated tester) starts typing commands at your OS. Appendix D explains what she does.

80.body: TypeScript has one numeric type, number, which is a 64-bit IEEE-754 floating-point value. It can hold integers exactly up to 2⁵³, so it's perfectly happy to hold 256, or 70 000, or −3. A 6502 register can't: it holds 8 bits, 0 to 255. So every time rObSen computes a register value, it has to force the result back into 8 bits. That's what & 0xff is for. (There's also bigint for arbitrarily large integers, and typed arrays like Uint8Array that store actual bytes. Memory uses a Uint8Array; the registers are plain numbers.)

81.body: 0xff, 0x300, 0xa9 are just numbers written in base 16. 0xff is 255, 0x100 is 256, 0x300 is 768. Hex is used because each hex digit is exactly 4 bits, so a byte is always two hex digits, which makes bit patterns visible: Hex Binary Decimal 0x0f 0000 1111 15 0xf0 1111 0000 240 0xff 1111 1111 255 0x80 1000 0000 128 0x100 1 0000 0000 256 You can also write binary literals (0b1111_0000) and use _ as a digit separator in any numeric literal.

82.body: JavaScript's bitwise operators convert their operands to 32-bit signed integers , operate bit by bit, and give back a 32-bit signed integer. Operator Name Example Result a & b AND: 1 where both are 1 0x1234 & 0xff 0x34 a | b OR: 1 where either is 1 0x12 << 8 | 0x34 0x1234 a ^ b XOR: 1 where they differ 0b1100 ^ 0b1010 0b0110 ~a NOT: flip every bit ~0 -1 a << n shift left, fill with 0 1 << 8 256 a >> n shift right, copy the sign bit -16 >> 2 -4 a >>> n shift right, fill with 0 (unsigned) -1 >>> 28 15

83.body: this.PC = (this.PC + 1) & 0xff; 0xff is eight 1-bits. ANDing with it keeps the low 8 bits of a number and zeroes everything above. So 0xff + 1 = 0x100, and 0x100 & 0xff = 0x00: the PC wraps from 255 to 0, exactly like an 8-bit register overflowing. The same mask appears in Memory.write (value & 0xff), opAddWithCarry ((this.Acc + value) & 0xff), and opIncrementAbsolute. Control.hex picks its mask by width: private static hex(value: number, width: number = 2): string { const mask = width > 2 ? 0xffff : 0xff; const normalized = (value ?? 0) & mask; return normalized.toString(16).toUpperCase().padStart(width, "0"); } Two hex digits get 0xff (one byte); four get 0xffff (two bytes). The ?? 0 turns undefined or null into 0 first (Chapter 6a).

84.body: private fetchWord(): number { this.ensureOperandAvailable(2); const low = _MemoryAccessor.read(this.PC & 0xff); const high = _MemoryAccessor.read((this.PC + 1) & 0xff); this.PC = (this.PC + 2) & 0xff; return ((high << 8) | low) & 0xffff; } Suppose memory holds 50 01 at the PC. Then low = 0x50, high = 0x01, and: high << 8 = 0x0100 (0000 0001 0000 0000) | low = 0x0150 (0000 0001 0101 0000) The shift moves the high byte up into bits 8–15, and OR drops the low byte into bits 0–7, which are known to be empty. The trailing & 0xffff is defensive: it guarantees a 16-bit result. Going the other way (splitting a word into bytes) is word & 0xff for the low byte and (word >> 8) & 0xff for the high byte. Because the low byte comes first in memory, this byte order is called little-endian . The RPC slide in Chapter 3 (p. 219) mentions "big-endian and little-endian" as one of the representation problems remote procedure calls have to solve.

85.body: A branch offset is one byte, but it has to mean "forward or backward." The convention is two's complement : a byte whose top bit is 0 (0x00–0x7f) is 0 to 127; a byte whose top bit is 1 (0x80–0xff) is the value minus 256, so −128 to −1. private opBranchNotEqual(): void { const offset = this.fetchByte(); if (this.Zflag !== 0) { return; } const signedOffset = offset < 0x80 ? offset : offset - 0x100; this.PC = (this.PC + signedOffset) & 0xff; } offset < 0x80 ? offset : offset - 0x100 is that rule, spelled out. 0xEF (239) becomes 239 − 256 = −17. A more compact (and more cryptic) way to sign-extend a byte uses the fact that bitwise operators work on 32-bit signed values: const signed = (offset << 24) >> 24; // move bit 7 into bit 31, then arithmetic-shift back The rObSen version is clearer. Alan's comment on rot13 applies: "There's a lot to be said for obvious code." Then (this.PC + signedOffset) & 0xff adds the offset and wraps. Branching backwards past 0 wraps to the top of the 256-byte space, as it would on 8-bit hardware.

const mem = new Uint8Array(4);
mem[0] = 256; // stored as 0
mem[1] = -1; // stored as 255
mem[2] = 3.9; // stored as 3 A Uint8Array converts whatever you store into an unsigned byte (modulo 256, truncating fractions). That's why Memory can't hold an out-of-range value even if someone forgot to mask. It's also why bugs involving typed arrays are quiet: nothing throws.

91.body: The host's Start button ends with _Kernel = new Kernel(); _Kernel.krnBootstrap();. Here is the bootstrap: public krnBootstrap() { this.enterKernelMode("Bootstrap"); // Page 8. { Control.hostLog("bootstrap", "host"); // Use hostLog because we ALWAYS want this, even if _Trace is off. // Initialize our global queues. _KernelInterruptQueue = new Queue(); // A (currently) non-priority queue for interrupt requests (IRQs). _KernelBuffers = new Array(); // Buffers... for the kernel. _KernelInputQueue = new Queue(); // Where device input lands before being processed out somewhere. _ReadyQueue = new Queue(); _Swapper = new Swapper(); // Initialize the console. _Console = new Console(); // The command line interface / console I/O device. _Console.init(); // Initialize standard input and output to the _Console. _StdIn = _Console; _StdOut = _Console; // Load the Keyboard Device Driver this.krnTrace("Loading the keyboard device driver."); _krnKeyboardDriver = new DeviceDriverKeyboard(); // Construct it. _krnKeyboardDriver.driverEntry(); // Call the driverEntry() initialization routine. this.krnTrace(_krnKeyboardDriver.status); // Load the Disk Device Driver this.krnTrace("Loading the disk device driver."); _krnDiskDriver = new DeviceDriverDisk(); _krnDiskDriver.driverEntry(); this.krnTrace(_krnDiskDriver.status); // // ... more? // // Enable the OS Interrupts. (Not the CPU clock interrupt, as that is done in the hardware sim.) this.krnTrace("Enabling the interrupts."); this.krnEnableInterrupts(); // Launch the shell. this.krnTrace("Creating and Launching the shell."); _OsShell = new Shell(); _OsShell.init(); // Finally, initiate student testing protocol. if (_GLaDOS) { _GLaDOS.afterStartup(); } this.exitToUserMode(); } In order: Enter kernel mode and log bootstrap with hostLog (not krnTrace, because this line should appear even if tracing is off). Build the kernel's queues. The interrupt queue holds pending interrupt requests. The input queue holds characters the keyboard driver has decoded. The ready queue holds processes waiting for the CPU. And a swapper for later. Create the console and point standard input and standard output at it. _StdIn and _StdOut are abstractions: everything else in the OS prints with _StdOut.putText and never needs to know it's a canvas. Load the device drivers : construct each one and call its driverEntry() initialization routine, then trace its status. (The disk driver's entry routine just sets status = "loaded"; it doesn't format anything. The disk is formatted lazily, the first time anything reads it.) Enable interrupts. Launch the shell , which prints the first prompt. Hand control to GLaDOS , if she's loaded, so she can start typing tests. Exit to user mode. Compare it with the slide's description of a bootstrap program: "Initializes all aspects of system. Loads operating system kernel and starts execution" (slide p. 25). In rObSen the browser has already loaded all the code (as <script> tags), so "loading the kernel" means constructing the Kernel object; the rest is initialization.

92.body:
public krnOnCPUClockPulse() { /* This gets called from the host hardware simulation every time there is a hardware clock pulse. This is NOT the same as a TIMER, which causes an interrupt and is handled like other interrupts. This, on the other hand, is the clock pulse from the hardware / VM / host that tells the kernel that it has to look for interrupts and process them if it finds any. */ // Check for an interrupt, if there are any. Page 560 if (_KernelInterruptQueue.getSize() > 0) { // Process the first interrupt on the interrupt queue. // TODO (maybe): Implement a priority queue based on the IRQ number/id to enforce interrupt priority. var interrupt = _KernelInterruptQueue.dequeue(); this.krnInterruptHandler(interrupt.irq, interrupt.params); } else if (_CPU.isExecuting) { // If there are no interrupts then run one CPU cycle if there is anything being processed. _CPU.cycle(); } else { // If there are no interrupts and there is nothing being executed then just be idle. this.krnTrace("Idle"); } Control.hostUpdateDisplays(); } This is the most important function in the OS, and it's 22 lines. Every 100 ms the host calls it, and it does exactly one of three things: If an interrupt is pending, handle one interrupt . Otherwise, if the CPU is executing, run one instruction . Otherwise, idle . Then it refreshes the displays. Interrupts always win. That's the right priority (an interrupt is something that needs attention now ), and it means a user program can't starve the keyboard: while you're typing, each keystroke costs the running program one instruction. It also means interrupts are handled only between instructions, never in the middle of one, which is how real CPUs behave and what the project spec requires. Interrupt priority
The comment says "TODO (maybe): Implement a priority queue based on the IRQ number/id to enforce interrupt priority." Right now the queue is first-in, first-out, so a keyboard interrupt that arrived first is handled before a timer interrupt that arrived second. Slide p. 36 says interrupt vectors are dispatched "based on priority," and some interrupts are "non-maskable." On real hardware the timer usually outranks the keyboard. Chapter 13a's generic priority queue would make this a two-line change. krnStep (used by the Step button) is the same logic, but called by hand, one tick at a time: public krnStep(): void { this.enterKernelMode("Step"); _OSclock++; if (_KernelInterruptQueue.getSize() > 0) { const interrupt = _KernelInterruptQueue.dequeue(); this.krnInterruptHandler(interrupt.irq, interrupt.params); } else if (_CPU && _CurrentProcess) { _CPU.step(); } else { this.krnTrace("Idle"); } Control.hostUpdateDisplays(); this.exitToUserMode(); }

94.body: public krnInterruptHandler(irq, params) { this.enterKernelMode("Interrupt"); // This is the Interrupt Handler Routine. See pages 8 and 560. // Trace our entrance here so we can compute Interrupt Latency by analyzing the log file later on. Page 766. this.krnTrace("Handling IRQ~" + irq); // Invoke the requested Interrupt Service Routine via Switch/Case rather than an Interrupt Vector. // TODO: Consider using an Interrupt Vector in the future. // Note: There is no need to "dismiss" or acknowledge the interrupts in our design here. // Maybe the hardware simulation will grow to support/require that in the future. switch (irq) { case TIMER_IRQ: this.krnTimerISR(); // Kernel built-in routine for timers (not the clock). break; case KEYBOARD_IRQ: _krnKeyboardDriver.isr(params); // Kernel mode device driver _StdIn.handleInput(); break; default: this.krnTrapError( "Invalid Interrupt Request. irq=" + irq + " params=[" + params + "]", ); } this.exitToUserMode(); } The interrupt handler (sometimes called the first-level interrupt handler, or the interrupt dispatcher) has one job: figure out which interrupt this is and call the right interrupt service routine (ISR) . rObSen does it with a switch on the IRQ number, as discussed in Chapter 1. TIMER_IRQ → krnTimerISR, the scheduler's entry point (Chapter 13). KEYBOARD_IRQ → the keyboard driver's ISR, which decodes the key and queues a character; then _StdIn.handleInput(), which drains the character queue into the console. That second call means console processing (echoing, line editing, and, when Enter is pressed, running the whole shell command) happens inside the keyboard interrupt. Real kernels split this into a fast "top half" that just queues the data and a deferred "bottom half" that processes it later. rObSen does both halves at once, which is simpler and fine for a single-user teaching OS. Anything else → krnTrapError: an unknown IRQ is a fatal error. The comment "There is no need to 'dismiss' or acknowledge the interrupts in our design" refers to a real hardware step: after servicing an interrupt, the OS must tell the interrupt controller it's done (an "end of interrupt" signal), or the controller won't deliver the next one. Dequeueing does that implicitly here. Slide p. 41: the kernel I/O structure. iP1 is the keyboard driver; iP4 is the disk driver.

95.body: private enterKernelMode(reason: string): void { _Mode = MODE_KERNEL; if (_Trace) { Control.hostLog(`Mode -> Kernel (${reason})`, "OS"); } _ModeDisplayUpdater?.(); } private exitToUserMode(): void { _Mode = MODE_USER; if (_Trace) { Control.hostLog("Mode -> User", "OS"); } _ModeDisplayUpdater?.(); } Every kernel entry point calls enterKernelMode(reason) on the way in and exitToUserMode() on the way out, and each transition is logged with its reason: Mode -> Kernel (Interrupt), Mode -> Kernel (Timer), Mode -> Kernel (Run PID). _ModeDisplayUpdater is a function pointer the host installs so the kernel can refresh the "Mode" cell in the CPU panel without knowing anything about the DOM. (?.() calls it only if it's been set; see Chapter 6a.) This is slide p. 54 made visible: "Dual-mode operation allows OS to protect itself… Mode bit provided by hardware… System call changes mode to kernel, return from call resets it to user." Two caveats, which follow from Chapter 1's observation that nothing checks the bit: Transitions nest without a stack. krnInterruptHandler enters kernel mode, calls krnTimerISR, which enters kernel mode again and exits to user mode before returning, after which the handler exits to user mode a second time. The final state is right, but for a moment inside the handler the bit says "user" while kernel code is still running. The kernel "exits to user mode" even when there's no user process to return to (for instance at the end of bootstrap and shutdown). On a real machine, "user mode with nothing running" would be the idle loop. A more faithful design would have the CPU set the mode: switch to kernel mode on any interrupt or trap, and switch to user mode only when dispatching a process. Then the bit would mean "is user code running?", which is exactly what the memory accessor needs to know (Chapter 4).

96.body: public krnShutdown() { this.enterKernelMode("Shutdown"); this.krnTrace("begin shutdown OS"); // TODO: Check for running processes. If there are some, alert and stop. Else... // ... Disable the Interrupts. this.krnTrace("Disabling the interrupts."); this.krnDisableInterrupts(); if (_CPU) { _CPU.isExecuting = false; } _CurrentProcess = null; if (_ReadyQueue) { _ReadyQueue.clear(); } Control.hostUpdateDisplays(); // // Unload the Device Drivers? // More? // this.krnTrace("end shutdown OS"); this.exitToUserMode(); } // trap the kernel (gpt generated) public krnTrap(reason: string): void { this.krnTrace("OS ERROR - TRAP: " + reason); if (_Console && _Console.showBSOD) { _Console.showBSOD(reason); } this.krnShutdown(); } krnShutdown disables interrupts, stops the CPU, clears the current process and the ready queue, and refreshes the displays. The comments are candid about what's missing: "TODO: Check for running processes. If there are some, alert and stop," and "Unload the Device Drivers? More?" The clock keeps ticking after a shutdown command (only Halt stops it), so the kernel goes on logging "Idle" with interrupts off, like a machine at a halt instruction. krnTrap(reason) is the fatal-error path: log, paint the Blue Screen, shut down. There's also an older krnTrapError(msg) further down, which logs and shuts down without the BSOD; its TODO, "Display error on console, perhaps in some sort of colored screen. (Maybe blue?)", is precisely what krnTrap later implemented (the comment above krnTrap says it was GPT-generated). An unknown IRQ still goes through the old one. Unifying them is a good small cleanup.

97.body: public krnTrace(msg: string) { // Check globals to see if trace is set ON. If so, then (maybe) log the message. if (_Trace) { if (msg === "Idle") { // We can't log every idle clock pulse because it would quickly lag the browser quickly. if (_OSclock % 10 == 0) { // Check the CPU_CLOCK_INTERVAL in globals.ts for an // idea of the tick rate and adjust this line accordingly. Control.hostLog(msg, "OS"); } } else { Control.hostLog(msg, "OS"); } } } The kernel's log calls all go through krnTrace, which respects the trace on|off shell command and throttles "Idle" to every tenth clock tick. Without the throttle, an idle OS would log ten lines a second forever and the textarea would bog down the browser.

98.body: Suppose GLaDOS enqueues 20 keyboard interrupts at once while a program is running. How many clock ticks pass before the program executes its next instruction? Why does the keyboard ISR call _StdIn.handleInput() immediately instead of leaving characters on the input queue for later? Where would you add a DISK_IRQ case, and what would the disk driver need to change for it to mean anything? Answers At least 20: each tick handles exactly one interrupt, and interrupts take priority over CPU cycles. Because nothing else would ever drain it. There's no separate "console process" or deferred-work mechanism; the interrupt handler is the only code that runs in response to input. (A bottom-half design would add a second queue check to krnOnCPUClockPulse.) In krnInterruptHandler's switch, calling _krnDiskDriver.isr(params). For it to mean anything, disk operations would have to be asynchronous : a request would start, return immediately, and the driver would raise DISK_IRQ when the operation "completes" (perhaps after a few simulated ticks of seek time). The requesting process would wait in a device queue meanwhile. Right now every disk call completes synchronously, so there's nothing to interrupt about.

99.body: TypeScript deep dive An operating system is mostly about things that might not be there. Is there a current process? Is the ready queue initialized yet? Did the memory manager find a free partition? Does this PID exist? The kernel answers "no" with null a lot, and TypeScript has a family of features for saying "this might be null" in a type and then handling it safely. rObSen uses all of them.
